#4054. Play as water and rain on wildfires in Atuel, a short, free game about the power and vulnerability of nature

Well, have you played Atuel? If not, you can do so within the next hour - it's a tiny, free, 25-minute walking sim, albeit one with little actual walking on account of you playing most of it as a river. More of a running sim, really.

Have You Played? is an endless stream of game retrospectives.

Technically, Atuel calls itself a "documentary game", and not without justification. While its sweeping Patagonian landscapes are rendered with a dreamy otherworldliness, and certain moments are downright mystic, the whole watery journey is based directly on the Atuel River that runs through western Argentina. As you drift downhill, taking control of water, clouds, and the local wildlife, you'll hear real-life scientists and historians monologuing on the Atuel and its relationship with the human cultures it's nourished. Mercifully, these are delivered with thoughtfulness as well as earnestness, maintaining the game's contemplative atmosphere without making it sound like the audio guide to a museum of Birmingham canals.

A few bends in, Atuel also takes on the climate crisis, directing you away from the soothing freshwater and into wildfires and parched riverbeds. I'd say this was preaching to the choir, at least for anyone who a) desires a functioning planet and b) learned about the water cycle in primary school, but then it isn't really preaching. Rather, developers Matajuegos weave between the beauty of the Earth and the need to protect it quite gracefully, and end their river tour on a more hopeful note than its darker moments may have intimated.

There's plenty else to leave an outsized impression in your memory matter: the understated, naturally-textured soundtrack, for instance, or the patiently gradual zoom-outs that slowly unveil the Andes' wild splendour. For me, and without wanting to undermine the importance or the accuracy of Atuel's environmental point, it was mainly just nice – therapeutic, even – to float through its gorgeous, surreal scenery like a cloud. And sometimes, as one. You can download it for free from Steam and Itch, with a pay-what-you-want option on the latter.

#4053. Silica, an FPS and RTS hybrid that mixes a smidge of Dune and Helldivers together, has left early access and entered 1.0

The concept of fusing an RTS and an FPS always sounds like a fun one, and since 2023 Martin Melichárek has been trying to make a new take on the combination under the watchful eye of DayZ devs Bohemia Interactive through Silica. Today marks the day that Silica leaves early access and enters 1.0, fully fleshing out its hybrid and mish mash of Dune's Arrakis and Helldivers' Terminids.

Digging into Silica a touch more deeply, it is a sci-fi shooter set on a planet where there's a fancy resource you're trying to mine that definitely isn't the spice. There are two warring factions competing for said resource, when, uh oh! Some bug-ish, giant aliens aren't very happy you're doing all that. So, you can either join the fray on the ground with some classic first-person shooting alongside your friends, or you can take the role of commander and dictate your artillery from above.

The 1.0 update obviously comes with a few additions, namely the Centauri Campaign, a "story-driven single-player experience set in the war for Baltarus. It opens with a cinematic intro and features fully voiced mission briefings and in-game dialogue. Between missions, a 3D planetary globe tracks the war as territory changes hands." Commanding your army should be a better experience now too, with the ability to "arrange units into formations, issue more precise movement and attack orders, and quickly select all units of the same type. Improved AI targeting and vehicle movement also help your armies operate more effectively in large-scale battles."

Beyond that, 1v1 matchmaking has been added in, where you can fight against another commander. The Steam Workshop sandbox tools have been expanded for building your own scenarios and sharing them with others. And there are a whole bunch of bug fixes, quality-of-life improvements and additions, and more. You can read about some of those in more detail in this handy little blog post. If you like what Silica is putting down, then you can pick it up on Steam.

25 OG Xbox titles are now on PC, and it's an utterly bizarre list of games

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

This weekend marks Xbox's 25th birthday, and while any celebration of the milestone is going to be muted in view of the layoff bloodbath Microsoft is currently engaging in, the gaming division is taking steps to keep us thinking about the brand in a positive light. That includes a fresh expansion to the list of original Xbox games that are now backwards compatible on PC.

After the four original Xbox games that Microsoft brought to PC earlier this year, another 21 have joined the list – a total of 25 games for the console's 25th birthday. The new list of games is an utterly bizarre one, largely dominated by LucasArts titles. That includes plenty of beloved Star Wars titles, alongside largely forgotten obscurities like Secret Weapons Over Normandy and Thrillville.

Some of the titles you might recognize, like Star Wars classics Battlefront 2, Jedi Outcast, and Knights of the Old Republic, are odd choices in themselves, since those games are already available on PC. Assuming Xbox is using the same emulation-based solution to port these games, they're all going to be substantially worse experiences than simply picking up the native PC versions for the same price on Steam.

That goes double for The Elder Scrolls 3: Morrowind, which is also on the list of newly added games. The Xbox version of Morrowind was a stunning technical achievement back in 2002, but it was notoriously janky even at the time, filled with bugs and technical limitations that have been robustly addressed on PC. I struggle to come up with a compelling reason anyone would want to play this version over the PC original today, especially with all the mods available for the RPG.

There are two games I absolutely will not complain about, however: TimeSplitters 2 and TimeSplitters: Future Perfect. Developed by the Rare veterans at Free Radical Design, the TimeSplitters series was a spiritual successor to classic N64 games GoldenEye and Perfect Dark, refreshing the FPS gameplay for a new generation with fun weapon gimmicks and charmingly goofy characters.

TimeSplitters never moved beyond cult classic status, and attempts to revive the series ended in failure. None of these games ever got PC ports, which makes their inclusion arguably the most notable part of this Xbox backwards compatibility update.

#4051. Fable's Latest Showing Didn't Exactly Blow Our Socks Off

It's the first time the Xbox RPG didn't wow us

Here at Pure Xbox, we're rather stoked about Playground Games' revival of Fable. We were picking jaws up off the floor in June, then again at gamescom in August, and even left London FanFest feeling pretty jazzed with what we got to play of the upcoming RPG.

So, let it been known for the record, I fully expect Fable to be a brilliant RPG. Top class in execution, full of joy and wow moments aplenty, but what on earth was Xbox thinking promoting Fable with that four-minute gameplay video? C'mon gang!

The footage was revealed during Seattle FanFest as part of Xbox's 25th anniversary jollies, although most of it was stuff we'd sorta seen before, and the choice of location was questionable at best. See for yourself in the video above.

"Both myself and Craig had a chance to play this demo last weekend, and we both came away pretty darn impressed with what we'd played. That said, we also remarked to each other that we wished we'd had a chance to explore Albion and interact with NPCs, which is something we'll have to wait a little bit longer for."

Feature We've Finally Played Xbox's New Fable Reboot, And Here's What We Think So Far

We went hands on at the recent Xbox FanFest

Where we'd previously been gobsmacked by vibrant castle towns and lush wilderness, this latest setting felt rather basic and lacking in character or detail. It was just some generic cliffside. It's not necessarily bad, but it's hardly the sort of environment I'd think to stuff into a trailer meant to turn people onto Fable.

As the video goes on, we get a little combat featuring swords, archery, and a sprinkling of magic. It all looks good, and having played the combat myself, it feels fun. But it doesn't last long, nor does it show us anything new or particularly interesting. The quest itself is cut short and lacking, as though it's just been ripped from a spoiler-free section of the game.

Just to reiterate, I reckon Fable will come good. Every gameplay reveal up until this point has been great. Big fan. This one just feels a little odd, almost as if it was cobbled together last minute. That's not ideal when you're trying to convince players to pick up Fable when it launches on Xbox Series X|S, PC, and PS5 on February 23, 2027.

#4050. The Citadel Project is a Thief-inspired dark fantasy, survival-horror lite stealth-em-up with some lovely shadows set in a medieval megastructure

You know, given the whole stealthy element of Thief-like immersive sims, I'm surprised there haven't been more of them with horror elements. There's Gloomwood, sure, but it's not as common as I'd like. That in turn then makes me curious about The Citadel Project, an immersive sim with some survival-horror elements set in a nasty, parasite-infected dark fantasy world, all apparently made by just one person.

In The Citadel Project, "the last line of defense built by the Ancient Kings in an attempt to preserve what remains of humanity in the face of the Great Storm." Some kind of evil force is ruining it from the inside, and you have to make your way through a medieval megastructure to figure out what happened. You aren't anyone special, "just a simple prisoner who manages to escape from a cell deep within the Citadel." Truthfully, the story sounds fine enough, I'm more smitten with the vibes put on display.

The shadows are what sells me, for the most part. They're dark and moody, looking plenty ripe for hiding in. And look, if you hand me a megastructure to explore, I'm going to do so. I'm also a fan of your main weapon, a crossbow. Not enough games with crossbows if you ask me! There's all sorts of bolts you can use with it, like a fire bolt that, obviously, sets things or enemies alight, a rope bolt to help you quickly climb or swing out of danger, a decoy bolt that makes a lot of sound to distract with, or a moss bolt; I'm not sure what that one does, my guess would be to dampen your footsteps and make it easier to sneak up on unsuspecting baddies.

Said baddies also appear to be infected with some kind of parasite, the severing of which appears to come in handy when trying to take them down. Overall, The Citadel Project likes a neat little im sim with just enough going on to make me curious to explore further. Which I might do, when I get the chance, as there is a demo available on Steam. Alternatively, I could just wait a week, as the game is out in early access November 11th, just over a week away. You can wishlist it on Steam right here.

#4049. Was This New Fable Gameplay Meant to Sell the Game?

I am pretty confident Fable will be a fantastic RPG when it finally releases in February 2027, but for those still sat on the fence, Xbox is going to have to do a better job of promoting it than this latest example.

To mark the 25th anniversary of Xbox, four minutes of gameplay taken from a quest has been uploaded. However, all of maybe 30 seconds of it actually has anything going on. Watch it above.

Obviously, you do indeed do a lot of walking during open world RPGs, but it's not something you usually feature much in marketing beats. That's what most of the latest gameplay slice for Fable is, though: walking.

Partway through, there is a combat sequence showing off swordfighting, archery, and magical abilities. It's over quickly, however, and then we're back to walking. The video then concludes with a cutscene lacking context as it's been plucked out of the full game to be seen online.

I grew up playing the three mainline Fable games on the Original Xbox and Xbox 360; I have very fond memories of this series, so I want the new rebooted instalment to do well. It'll need better presentations and trailers than this for a good chance at that. It's out for PS5, Xbox Series X|S, and PC on 23rd February 2027.

#4048. How Nvidia got into this mess: timeline of Jensen Huang scandal and geopolitics leading up to it

We're hearing a lot more about this now, but this story didn't totally begin with Jensen's admission of an affair.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nvidia is the talk of the world right now. The company's co-founder Jensen Huang has been ousted from the company, following claims of multiple affairs: one said to be with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, and another an alleged with an executive at Nvidia.

These events and more had put pressure on the company's board to consider ousting the co-founder and CEO, who has now been replaced by CFO Colette Kress acting as interim CEO; at least until a suitable replacement can be found.

To better understand these events, the wider context of what's at stake, and why chip smuggling and export controls are also a part of the conversation, check out our timeline below.

New York Times report on Jensen Huang's unclear relationship with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang.

Alice Huang was the managing director of Megaspeed, a datacentre company in Singapore that imported billions of dollars worth of Nvidia GPUs. Her husband, Kang Wei, is a private equity investor.

Megaspeed had been subject to an investigation for chip smuggling, but Nvidia and the company say it was cleared of suspicion.

Megaspeed statement from December, 25: "We want to be absolutely clear: over the past six months, our company has undergone multiple on-site inspections and reviews by key institutions, including the Bureau of Industry and Security of the US Commerce Department, the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry of Malaysia, and Nvidia. These thorough investigations have confirmed that there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities."

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

Nvidia spokesperson, John Rizzo, said at the time accusations of chip smuggling made against Megaspeed were "thoroughly investigated and debunked last year."

However, during that investigation, Alice Huang is said to have come under suspicion by US authorities, who determined that Alice Huang was working as an intelligence asset for China.

Authorities also noted Jensen Huang was close to Alice Huang, though their exact relationship was not specified.

Rizzo said: “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”

It is said at this time that neither Jensen nor Nvidia had been briefed on foreign intelligence threats by the US government, despite prior memos in the government and US authorities deeming her a threat.

Jensen is called to a meeting with the various national security and foreign affairs committee leaders in US Congress on November 18.

On the meeting for this agenda is Alice Huang: Jensen's relationship with her and whether she could have collected sensitive information about US technology. It's also about Nvidia's security protocols.

This presumably puts some pressure on Huang and Nvidia to be seen to take action.

Jensen Huang and Nvidia's board put out statements at the same time on Nvidia's newsroom.

Jensen's statement admits he was having an affair with an unnamed person. He apologises to wife and family, his staff, and says he has fallen short of his responsibility to them.

In the same statement, he notes national security concerns arising from news reports:

"Nvidia’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American."

The board of Nvidia focuses on the reports of a "foreign intelligence effort" against the company's CEO and launches an independent investigation to check.

"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information. Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it."

The share price for Nvidia drops: around 21% since October 28, the day prior to the initial New York Times report.

This also happens to be around a similar time of a wider tech selloff due to AI fears, midterm elections, and opposition to datacentres.

Nvidia loses a couple hundred billion dollars in value, give or take. It's share price is not quite the lowest it's been this year—that was on March 30. That was driven by fears of AI spending slowing, CapEx, and China export rules. So it's not apocalyptic for the company.

Donald Trump speaks to press about his pal, Jensen Huang. He's generally very positive and seems to back the Nvidia CEO.

Trump asked if Jensen Huang had any idea Alice Huang was a spy. Jensen Huang said no.

Trump was reportedly informed of Alice Huang much earlier, but suggested he did not regret not acting on that advice sooner: "No, I don't think so. I think he's an honourable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it."

"He's an amazing guy. I just hope there's no problem. If there is a problem, we'll let you know about it."

Trump also casually mentions the FBI are investigating.

Law firms start flooding in with requests for Nvidia investors to sign up to class-action lawsuits or "investigations" into the company. I saw around five press releases for law firms offering their services to investors hoping to claim back some money, but there are reportedly even more.

The Rosen Law Firm's complaint (PDF) outlines ways that Nvidia may have made misleading or false statements on Jensen Huang, his relationship with Alice Huang, and didn't express the risks to the company and share price adequately.

Nvidia hires law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead Jensen Huang affair probe.

Report by The Information suggests Alice Huang facilitated some 240k AI GPUs, largely at-the-time banned H100 and H200 chips, roughly costing around $7.5B

It is speculated that Alice Huang was introduced to Jensen Huang by her investor husband, who had interest in gaming companies. It is also speculated whether she was picked up by Chinese intelligence after starting a relationship with Huang, rather than the other way around.

Axios reports that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was sent a classified memo warning over the relationship between Jensun and Alice Huang. Lutnick is the one charged with safeguarding US technology and keeping it away from its perceived rivals.

The report also notes that Marco Rubio warned Trump about Huang being potentially spied upon on Airforce 1 directly before they picked up Jen-Hsun for the China trip.

Huang returns to a "sad" Nvidia office but seems to act business as usual.

"… If the worst thing he did in real life is infidelity with ⁠this woman who may or may not be a Chinese spy—but she might be—that's enough, because whatever else there is, we don't know. And to me, that's a security risk."

Jensen Huang claimed to have yet another affair, this time it is alleged with someone at Nvidia: vice president Kimberly Powell. The Nvidia board meets in claimed preparation to oust Huang.

The New York Times cites five unnamed sources, claiming they were made aware of the affair. It was also claimed the pair were seen "being affectionate" at an Nvidia conference earlier this year, and a bystander recorded a video of the incident before being made an offer by security to sign an NDA.

The Wall Street Journal reports that the Nvidia board, currently setting up an investigation into their CEO, is meeting to discuss Jensen Huang's future. The report states the board is "preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang."

Nvidia's share price plummets in after-hours trading to its lowest value since June, 2025.

Jensen Huang has resigned from his position as CEO of Nvidia, effective immediately.

A statement on the Nvidia newsroom confirms Huang's departure. He has also vacated his seat on the board and role as president.

He will be replaced by interim CEO, Colette Kress, who had previously worked as the company's CFO for a long stretch.

"Nvidia Board of Directors announced today that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, Chief Executive Officer, and a member of the Board, effective immediately," a statement on Nvidia's newsroom says.

Export rules between the US and China go back to Biden and that administration's trade war. The US had previously blocked China from accessing the latest in lithographic chipmaking machines, but started to go further into exports of high-end chips.

In 2022, the US decided to halt exports of the very best datacentre chips to China, followed by limitations to the export of other certain GPUs from October, 2023. This bans the RTX 4090 and other capable cards based on performance density and total processing power.

Nvidia and AMD circumvent the ban with chips with limits to slide in under the new regulations, ie. the H20 and MI308. The secretary of commerce at the time, Gina Raimondo, didn't like that much.

Jensen Huang and AMD CEO Dr. Lisa Su say Chinese business is pretty much dried up during this period; Huang says company is "100% out of China."

Once Donald Trump is back in the White House, he proclaims a new policy that will "identify and eliminate loopholes in existing export controls." Later that same year, the president allows sale of some GPUs to China in return for 15% of AMD and Nvidia's China revenue.

By December, 2025, Trump says they can sell even the big chips, like the Hopper H200, but falls short of new Blackwell chips. US Commerce Department gets a 25% slice of the pie in return.

Chinese companies, like Alibaba and Bytedance, may be limited to 75,000 chips each. Nevertheless, Nvidia says it has lots of customers hoping for chips in China.

By February, 2026, sale of Nvidia's top chips are seemingly stalled by a national security review. US politicians are split on whether they should sell chips to China.

This seems to clear up, though, as recent NYT report suggests the US is approving sales of Nvidia AI chips to companies in China. Only problem is those companies are alleged to have dubious backgrounds and funding, thus further stoking some politicians' concerns that the US shouldn't be selling the chips to China whatsoever.

Turns out, China doesn't even want 'em. The CCP takes a while to agree to import the chips, then finally approves their import, then sorta backtracks, and reports suggest they're still stuck in Hong Kong to this day.

China wants homegrown tech. It wants to make its own chips, own chipmaking machines, and lessen dependence on the US—which makes sense, as for the past half-decade, it couldn't reliably get hold of advanced US chips; longer still, advanced lithographic machines.

So, for the better part of five years, and the AI boom, Chinese companies can't officially get their hands on many top AI chips.

Some chose to bypass export controls put in place by successive US administrations. This has led to counts and convictions for chip smuggling over the years.

GPU shipments in south east Asia have come under particular scrutiny, due to suspicions countries there have been used to indirectly ship chips to China.

There have been multiple high-value cases in Malaysia, Singapore, and Taiwan, using techniques such as dummy servers, swapping stickers with hairdryers, and diverting shipments. One case involving billions of dollars of hardware involves the co-founder of Supermicro, a datacentre server company.

The issue got so bad, the US government asked Malaysia to keep a close eye on any shipment containing Nvidia GPUs back in March, 2025.

Megaspeed was also subject to investigation going back to 2024. The NYT reports that the Commerce department's investigation into the company was later handed over to the Justice department, who is said to still be conducting a criminal inquiry into the company.

Officials cited in the story suggest Nvidia's involvement in the case to be strange. Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said the company works "to help government and our partners halt any would-be smugglers while serving the critical market of lawful customers that help America win worldwide."

By December, 2025, Megaspeed published a statement on its website denying any claims of chip smuggling, citing inspections by multiple authorities and Nvidia. Nvidia also backs the company's legitimacy.

NEW: We are short Nvidia $NVDA. We believe Nvidia has a significant China problem. Please see our full report and disclosures now available on our website, link in bio. https://t.co/oTaJyL7S2RMay 13, 2026

A later report by Culper Research alleges Megaspeed is financed in part by Chinese giant Alibaba through a shell company. Megaspeed's balance sheet is said to have exploded from $33 million at the end of 2023 to $3 billion by the end of 2024, and its subsidiary, Speedmatrix, imported billions of dollars' worth of products from an Nvidia server company.

There are further claims made of companies, shell companies, subsidiaries, being set up and moving shipments around the region. Though a great deal of speculation remains as to where any chips actually ended up.

That said, the US government holds that DeepSeek has been trained on Blackwell GPUs, which technically it shouldn't have been able to access—a claim that Nvidia later suggested it could not substantiate.

"We haven’t seen any substantiation or received tips of ‘phantom data centers’ constructed to deceive us and our partners, then deconstructed, smuggled and reconstructed somewhere else,” an Nvidia spokesperson said at the time.

"While such smuggling seems far-fetched, we pursue any tip we receive."

#4047. "Steam's review queue is clogged up by AI slop": Salacious Fire Emblem-ish Food Devils gets a delay because its devs think Valve is inundated with genAI games

You might have seen that for today's grub, Edwin decided to in part feed The Maw with Food Devils, an incredibly salacious, foodie take on Fire Emblem, as it was meant to release today. The only problem is, it's not actually out yet. That might prompt you to call Edwin a rotten liar and march up to his castle at the top of the hill on a dark and stormy night with pitchforks and torches, but I beseech you to wait, because it's actually Steam's fault. And potentially, it's the fault of all those awful AI games that have been flooding Steam recently.

In a Steam blog post shared earlier today, developer Studio Daimon explained why the game isn't able to be released today, first offering a bit of context: if you want to put your game on Steam, you have to submit for approval so that it matches what you've described and doesn't harbour malware, amongst other reasons. As the post explains, "before submitting a build, devs see a disclaimer that says 'This review typically takes 3-5 business days, but please allow up to 7 business days in case feedback needs to be addressed'." Except the team submitted their build on October 12th, more than 20 days ago, with no approval in sight.

The reason? "We can only assume it's because Steam's review queue is clogged up by AI slop, but the whole process is now taking several weeks for some developers." For some context, Game Discovery Tool did some statistics magic and found that more than 50% of games released in October on Steam featured an AI disclosure. Valve have required that games disclose AI use since January 2024, and a year on from then in January 2025 only just over 14% of games featured such a disclosure. In January 2026, that jumped up to a little over 25%, and now here we are at more than 50%.

And to be clear, Steam releases have gone up too. According to SteamDB data, a little over 2000 games were released on the platform in October 2025. But in October 2026, that has jumped up to almost 4000. Correlation is obviously not causation, so take that with a pinch of salt. Still, it paints a concerning image over AI usage, and potentially sounds like it's affecting how Valve operates. Almost as if allowing free reign over AI is bad, or something!

Unfortunately for Studio Daimon, there's no estimate on when Food Devils might launch. "Even now, we don't know when Steam will give us the final OK to finally release our game," they wrote. "We sent another ticket last week saying that the situation was urgent and that we might miss our release date because of this, but it also got ignored. I'm sure that their staff is just too overwhelmed at the moment, but these sudden and massive delays have affected many developers throughout October, with some even being forced to postpone their releases... including us."

They're hoping to still be able to release it by the end of the week, but "can't make any plans or promises because it's out of our control." Perhaps in the meantime, for those who like what's cooking in the devs' kitchen, we could throw the game a wishlist to be ready for whenever it does launch.

#4046. Ubisoft are reportedly tapped as one potential company that could acquire Arkane, though the Dishonored studio's own management may be in the running too

I'd really like it if it weren't Ubisoft though

Things are potentially looking up for Arkane, depending on how you feel about Ubisoft (and depending on who actually ends up acquiring them). I mention the Assassin's Creed developer because, reportedly, they're interested in buying the studio from Microsoft, having even made a bid for it. I'll go out on a limb here and say it's the whole being French thing, but uh, I'd really rather someone else bought Arkane.

This comes from, you guessed it, Bloomberg, who say that sources they've spoken with claim two other gaming companies have also made a bit. There is even the potential that Arkane would be sold to their own management, as Xbox are considering such a move. But overall, it doesn't yet sound like anything is leaning any particular way, as Xbox haven't formalised a deal with any of the potential buyers. Bloomberg also note that if a deal is made, this should then allow Arkane to finish their work on their Blade game, which is expected to release within the next couple of years.

Apparently an Xbox spokesperson told Bloomberg that the gaming company is exploring their options ahead of their December deadline, but didn't comment any further. Ubisoft reportedly did not have a comment to make on the matter. For some context on that December deadline, because of French labour laws, companies that have over 1000 staff members are required to search for a buyer for three months before they can just completely shut down. That makes December 13th the final date that such a deal has to be made by, meaning there's about a month and a half left to go.

Arkane's sale comes as part of a sweeping range of cuts, sales and closures being made by Microsoft at the moment. In July, it was announced that studios like Double Fine, Undead Labs and Compulsion would no longer be a part of Xbox, with all three going indie; Ninja Theory was also announced as part of these cuts, but unfortunately it's looking like they'll be shutting their doors. Thousands of Xbox staff were also laid off at this time, with more laid off in September, and even more coming this month and January reportedly. As always, solidarity with all workers affected by Microsoft's heartless and money hungry cuts.

Playground Games is ramping up its marketing efforts for its upcoming Fable revival, and a new gameplay showcase seems to confirm the return of enemy Nymphs, which we haven't seen since the original Fable back in 2004.

The new Official Quest Gameplay trailer, released as part of Xbox's 25th anniversary shenanigans, shows a darker side to Albion than we're used to seeing, and I mean that literally. After cranking up the brightness on my monitor, I could see that the footage shows a female hero character seeking out her village's mysterious assailant with the help of a character named Arden. Tracing the attacker's path leads the duo through a heavily wooded forest with giant thorny vines and eventually, a confrontation with some familiar-looking foes outside a cave entrance.

Again, everything is dark in this trailer, but from what I can tell these fellas look a whole lot like the Wood Nymphs, which are one of two species of fairy-like creatures, the other being Water Nymphs, from OG Fable back in the day. They're referred to as "cursed monsters" in the quest log, but c'mon, those are fairies. They're little magical winged humanoids with big heads and tree bark-like skin, and they flutter around in clouds of colorful orbs and shoot ethereal projectiles your way. If that isn't a Wood Nymph, well then I don't know what a Wood Nymph is. And believe me, I know a thing or two about Wood Nymphs.

Anyway, otherwise the trailer is fairly unremarkable. Not in a bad way, just in a way that doesn't reveal anything super new or exciting to talk about, which makes sense considering we're just a few short months away from getting to play the game. Fable is out on PS5, Xbox Series X, and PC on February 23.

#4044. "An outright ban will not eliminate AI from the modding process," Nexus Mods say as they rule out barring generated creations from their site

"We drew the line where the real argument is"

The owners of Nexus Mods have ruled out instituting an outright ban on AI-generated works being uploaded the site, instead opting to expand their current rules on modders disclosing how they've used AI in making their mods. This latest move to address the waves of AI-created or AI-thumbnailed mods now hitting Nexus Mods on a daily basis follows Nexus' modus operandi up to this point, which has been simply to try and ensure AI usage is clearly labelled so prospective downloaders can make informed decisions.

"We won't introduce an outright ban on AI-generated mods," Nexus Mods owner and CEO Victor 'Foledinho' Folmann wrote in a news post. "You may ask me why, since that is not the solution some of you were looking for. The answer is simple: AI is currently used throughout the whole process of creation, from script autocompletion to generation of textures, voices, and full assets, and it is difficult to draw a clear boundary between what is acceptable and unacceptable. An outright ban will not eliminate AI from the modding process, but will prevent people from mentioning its use. We'd prefer the opposite; it should be out in the open, clearly labelled, and regulated according to the rules that we can implement on our platform.

"This doesn't mean that any work done using AI will get removed; AI-generated mods are welcome on our platform provided that they meet certain criteria regarding permissions, transparency, presentation, and conduct. Mod Authors should have a chance to decide about the further use of their work, and you should be able to decide for yourselves how much AI-based content you want to see, whether more, less, or no content at all.

"As for our own position: Nexus Mods will not use your mods to train AI and will not sell or license them to anyone doing so. We refused to do that in the past, and we will refuse to do so in the future. Given such a variety of opinions within our community, not everyone will agree with any decision taken. These are the ones we believe are right for Nexus Mods today, and we’ll keep adjusting them as the tools evolve and as we see how these changes work in practice, with your feedback guiding that."

In terms of the changes which are being brought in to toughen up the site's current three tag system design to make mods containing AI-generated content, AI media, or made with AI assistance easier to spot, Nexus are making AI disclosures mandatory for those uploading new mods. "What this means is that for mods tagged as AI-assisted, we’re also introducing a requirement for a public explanation of how and where AI was used, which should give you a better understanding of what you’re downloading, rather than leaving you to make assumptions on a tag alone," Folmann wrote. "We’re also going to make AI tags on mod pages more prominent, displaying them immediately after adult-content tags so they’re easier to spot."

"While we hope these changes will encourage everyone to disclose their AI usage, to be honest, that’s not going to happen," he continued. "Additionally, we are putting clear moderation standards in place, enforced with consequences for breaking the rules." New "permission options covering AI usage and training, as well as forks and derivative mods" are also being worked on, with the hopes of giving modders more control over how their works can be reused. Finally, Folmann noted that the site are "investing in security tooling and specialised staff" to address concerns over generative AI making "bespoke malicious code hidden inside mods" more prevalent.

Mod makers are being given a 60 day grace period to make sure their existing works meet the new rules, which'll run until January 2nd.

As you can imagine, the comments section of this Nexus Mods announcement is lively. Over on LinkedIn, Folmann patted himself on the back a bit about the mixed reception being an indicator the site are going about this the right way. "Some wanted a full ban. Some think we went too far. That tells me we drew the line where the real argument is," he declared, adding that "transparency beats prohibition". He also reiterated that his vision is of "modding that's Spotify-easy to play and GitHub-powerful to create, with humans in charge".

I reckon that with or without these changes, in the absence of its owners taking a strong stand browsing Nexus Mods is going to carry on be more of an exercise in ducking dodgy stuff than it was prior to most games' pages being splattered with the likes of icky AI-baked Geralt clones standing where decent screenshots of the actual game would've been more than adequate.

#4043. 'That's An Error' - Xbox Engineer Denies 360 Games Are Being Teased For Disc To Digital

Update [Fri 13th Nov 2026, 5:45pm]: Well, unfortunately we have answer - Xbox engineer Eden Marie has confirmed over on BlueSky that the inclusion of Fable III in this image was an "error".

While the post itself is private, it reads as follows (and thanks to Pure Xbox user TheBillConiglio for alerting us to this):

"Bill: Seeing an image of a library with Fable 3 having a disc to digital badge. Error, or......"

Original Story: Yesterday, Xbox starting rolling out three new console features for Xbox Insiders to try out: rotating home backgrounds, the ability to choose which side the Xbox guide pops open on, and new ways to organise disc to digital games.

They're all cool features that we're definitely keen to play around with, but what got our attention most was the image Xbox used to show off the new disc to digital update. Particularly, the games featured with the D2D licence icon plopped in the bottom-left corner of each game tile.

Did Xbox just tease the inclusion of Xbox 360 games in the D2D programme? Well, that would be true if the image depicting Fable III is to be taken at face value. At a glance, you'd probably see the image above and think, 'great, that's awesome', but the more you look at it, the weirder it gets.

Avowed famously launched on Xbox without a physical disc. So, if the theory about Xbox 360 games joining the programme is on the money, does that mean we're getting a physical copy of Avowed too? And what about Age of Empires IV? That never received a physical release either. Then If we really want to go Enola Holmes on this image, Forza games aren't D2D compatible.

We're thinking someone at Xbox might've messed up with this image. Announcements of this magnitude shouldn't be buried in an Xbox Insider update. Xbox should be shouting about it on the front page. So, why do an Xbox 360 game and two digital-only titles have D2D icons attached to them? I could think of a lazy reason.

Only time will tell, but consider us sceptical for now. We've chalked this one up to a blunder from Xbox, although it wouldn't surprise us if Xbox 360 games did eventually join the D2D programme. And hey, it's Xbox's birthday this Sunday. Maybe there's more to this than meets the eye.

#4042. DOOM: The Dark Ages and Horde Mode Is a Match Made in Heaven

Available for DLC owners from 16th November

id Software has revealed it's updating DOOM: The Dark Ages with a horde mode next week, called Slaughter Mode. It's a free addition, but there's a catch: you have to own this year's Revelations expansion to access it.

Slaughter Mode releases on Monday, 16th November 2026, and brings with it "an all-new endless survival challenge designed to put even the most seasoned Slayers to the test". It's got randomised enemies, bosses, and arenas, and the ability to record your personal high scores and compete in weekly challenges.

The trailer confirms there are 19 arenas in total, and every round of every run features a new combination of enemies to defeat. At checkpoints, you can cash out your total earnings so far in exchange for rewards. Or, you can risk losing everything by continuing your run and trying for a higher score.

You'll mostly be unlocking new character and weapon skins, profile icons, and music.

Review DOOM: The Dark Ages (PS5) - Medieval Mashup Slows Down for FPS Excellence

As an aside, Xbox boss Asha Sharma also confirmed developer id Software is also now working on its next game:

The DOOM series offers some of the best combat experiences and scenarios in all of video games, so being able to play it over and over again in a horde mode sounds perfect. This looks to be the full Dark Ages combat system placed into Slaughter Mode, so after a fantastic base game and supposedly even better DLC in Revelations, the title provides even more reason to return.

Will you check out Slaughter Mode next week? Let us know in the comments below.

So I've been utterly consumed by WoW: Forever, which is a relief, because it's my job to write about it—and I've been powering ahead to 40, where a deeply oldschool grind to get my first mount awaits me. Before that, though, I had an absolutely lovely time futzing around The Riverglades, one of WoW: Forever's properly bespoke zones. As in, this thing wasn't in vanilla. This was cooked up and released in November.

Having quested through most of it in a blissful fugue state with some friends, we each came to the conclusion that it all feels very 2007, rather than 2006.

The Riverglades, which you can head to at about level 38, is saturated with quests. Even more so than the revamped and revisited zones from vanilla World of Warcraft. And while it absolutely has the classic zone's sense of scale, and none of these quests have the retail aura of on-rails cutscenes about them, I wasn't actually tasting vanilla.

One of the hallmarks of older, classic-style quest design is a bunch of disparate quests that have you scattering out towards the map—Riverglades, then, feels a lot more modern, in that it uses that scattershot point-of-interest guide as a baseline, then cleverly tucks away even more quests at your destination.

In one case, fighting through a ruined village flooded with Twilight's Blade, me and my compatriot saw a quest marker underground. It took ages for us to find a basement, which then yawned out into an open cavern with shadow-infused ogres and a cunning woman trapped in a cage with her own quest chain.

At which point it clicked: Oh, I'm playing The Burning Crusade again. The template was classic, sure, but the density and the branching paths and the clever redirects—that's all Outland, baby. There's even a set of swampy flats in the middle of The Riverglades pock-marked by orcish poachers that made me say, out loud: Oh, I'm in Nagrand again. Just without the floating islands.

And you know what, having had this unexpectedly adjacent nostalgic experience, I didn't hate it.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

I do hope that Forever manages to preserve its more Vanilla aspects; I've written on this site quite recently about how I've adored just going on an adventure. Heck, I had the terrible idea to do the Scarlet Monastery as Alliance recently, and the quest chain leading up to the sword I wanted forced me to run all the way across Desolace to fight level 40 skeletons. It was great.

But The Burning Crusade, in many senses, was the best of both worlds. WoW hadn't been claimed by its Cataclysm-era propensity for goofs and pop culture references over atmosphere yet, but it also hadn't stuck doggedly to its vanilla quest design that was sometimes just flat-out bad.

In fact, many of Forever's new quests, even in other zones, have been built around plugging up awkward questing gaps, or giving players more to do in zones that've been otherwise barren. Which, as it turns out, just produces Outland 2.0. If the other levelling zones Blizzard adds to Forever are as Nagrand-flavoured as the Riverglades, I really don't mind at all.

#4040. Smash hit cyberpunk storekeeper Probably Stolen was originally a different, non-cyberpunk game that seemed destined to sink without trace

Publisher tinyBuild celebrates turnaround after very underwhelming demo numbers

Space station trading game Probably Stolen – Cyberpunk Shopkeeper Sim has been doing rather well on Steam, attracting over 162,000 concurrent players last night. I've been feeling the urge to fire it up again myself, after my brief launch-day trawl through its quagmire of black market economics and factional rivalries.

The game's big numbers come as a shock given that it began life as another, non-cyberpunk kiosk job sim called Deepspace Emporium, which still has a Steam page as of writing. Deepspace Emporium seemed doomed to fizzle out in obscurity. But publisher tinyBuild got behind it regardless, working with developers Questing Goose to overhaul the art direction and lay on extra brainchips. The gamble paid off.

"Probably Stolen was initially a game under a different name with a released demo," summarises tinyBuild CEO Alex Nichiporchik on Twitter. "That demo peaked at 28 concurrent players. We loved the concept and gameplay, and worked with the dev to reinvent the visuals and focus on what works design wise. This is the result."

The original Deepspace Emporium seems very similar to Probably Stolen in broad strokes. The core of the game is haggling with strung-out ne'er-do-wells, buying or selling goods of varying quality and legality in order to surf a fluctuating market and pay the rent. It's Papers, Please, but you're searching for fake watermarks on cigarette packets, and wondering whether you dare stock contraband weaponry. You also have to appease or outmanouevre factions with competing interests, from station security to underworld barons.

From what I've played, Probably Stolen essentially takes all that and pumps up the Netrunner parallels with posher visuals. Not having played the now-unavailable Deepspace demo, I can't say how much intrigue it adds to all the shady transactions going on beneath the hood.

I'm not blown away by Probably Stolen's pixelart – I find it quite flavourless, as depictions of cyberpunk space stations go – but it has pleasing texture. I am disproportionately fond of the rolled-up sleeping mat beneath my counter. Looks nicely padded! Still, the meat of this game is undoubtedly the vast collection of items you can get your greasy fingers on, with a choice of retail lines and vocational pathways such as gunsmith and chemist. You can sell rat corpses, tins of caviar, robotic hands, scavenged shotguns, and purple tubers of uncertain origin. I am Commander Silverhand, and this is my favourite store on the Citadel.

It's lovely to think of a developer transforming a probable write-off into a chart-topper by means of some canny plumping and reorganising. The situation is almost certainly more complicated than Nichiporchik makes it sound. Still, let's take the opportunity to reminisce moist-eyed about a few other games that underwent a dramatic visual transformation during development.

The obvious one is Team Fortress 2, which once upon a time looked like a prototype Silent Hill environment with some khaki toy soldiers. Gearbox worked similar sorcery upon Borderlands, which once looked like a hungover Fallout 3. The prevailing wisdom is that piping in some colour and whimsy propelled these games to greatness, but who knows, perhaps if they'd clung to the old "football stadium toilet bowl" vibe, they'd have made an extra billion apiece. Any other precedents come to your mind?

#4039. Kevin Feige says Doctor Doom isn't a variant of Tony Stark

Avengers: Doomsday hits theaters in a little over one month

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Kevin Feige says Doctor Doom isn't a variant of Tony Stark... despite that confusing Avengers: Endgame Encore post-credits scene making us think otherwise.

"People wondered, ‘Is Doom just a variant of another character? Is this just a shortcut to bringing back another character?’ The answer is no. He’s Victor Von Doom," Feige told Empire.

In one of several post-credits scenes that were added to the re-release of Avengers: Doomsday, Tony Stark is seen forging what appears to be a Doctor Doom mask. How are we not supposed to think that this implies Tony and Victor Von Doom are one and the same (aside from being played by the same actor)?

Even Variety posed a theory a little while ago that Doctor Doom is a variant of Iron Man from another planet, but it must be said again that Victor Von Doom and Tony Stark are completely separate characters in the comics. They go head-to-head in the 2008 comic book Iron Man: Legacy of Doom (which Downey was seen reading as part of his Doomsday prep). I hear you, though: How is the movie going to explain away Tony Stark and Doom having the same face? Well, he's rarely ever unmasked in the comics... so I just kind of figured the Russos were going to rely heavily on that. We'll see come December.

Avengers: Doomsday hits theaters in the UK on December 16 and in the US on December 18. For more, check out our guides to the Marvel timeline and how to watch the Marvel movies in order.

#4038. Wolfenstein 3 Announced, Now in the Works at MachineGames

MachineGames has officially confirmed it's now working on Wolfenstein 3.

As part of the 25th anniversary celebrations for Xbox, the developer and Asha Sharma posted word on social media.

The Swedish studio went with: "His reputation precedes him. Wolfenstein 3 is in production." Sharma, meanwhile, said: "Wolfenstein 3 is officially in production at MachineGames. One of gaming's most important franchises, and a team that has done remarkable work bringing it forward. Looking forward to sharing more."

In the post below, you can see the opening lines of the script, with chapter one called "Nazitraz". There is also a picture taken from the motion capture studio on the MachineGames tweet:

The team returns to the FPS series, having made the two most recent mainline games: Wolfenstein: The New Order and Wolfenstein II: The New Colossus (let's just forget about Wolfenstein Youngblood). It took a break from the franchise with Indiana Jones and the Great Circle, but now it's back to kill more Nazis.

At this stage (and it's presumably an early one), there's no word on whether Wolfenstein 3 is a multi-platform release or an Xbox exclusive. It's probably still at least a few years away from releasing.

Nevertheless, are you excited for the next B.J. Blazkowicz adventure? Let us know in the comments below.

#4036. Former Xbox First-Party Game 'Kiln' Gets A New Identity And Its Biggest Update Of All Time

When Double Fine released Kiln as an Xbox first-party title last year, it's fair to say a lot of the Xbox fanbase was baffled by it. As much as it was a good game (we gave it a 7/10 in our Pure Xbox review), it also shipped with just a singular, online-only mode that was bound to get old pretty quickly.

Double Fine ended up being let go by Xbox, turning Kiln from an Xbox first-party game into an independent game, and it received a brand-new update back in September, adding a new creative game mode along with various other features.

But today, to mark the planned end of development, it's received its biggest update of all time - adding in three new game modes, an increased level cap, a Photo Booth and loads more besides.

Here's a look at just the highlights of this new update:

In terms of the three modes, Fire Fighter is a 4v4 mode where "both teams are in a mad dash to catch a flaming Chimenea", Stoked is also a 4v4 mode that's "all about igniting the Pyres with your team’s flame", and Local Mini Quench is a smaller version of the original Quench mode that can be played with up to three other people offline.

Offline mode is actually classed as a separate new feature as well:

"As part of being able to play locally, we’ve added an offline mode. This allows you to play and practice without needing to worry about your Ping or people. This, alongside the player hosted matches and account change, helps future-proof Kiln so that you can play it for years to come!"

Pretty cool, right? On top of that, Kiln has received a brand-new identity this week in the form of "Kiln: Reshaped", with the name change serving as a way to "let you know how much is in this update!".

Unfortunately, it does seem like Kiln's flame has already been doused for the majority of players at this point, but it's great to see Double Fine putting in the work to not only preserve it for the future, but hopefully light the spark once again for people who have fallen away from it in recent months.

Don't forget it's on Xbox Game Pass as well, or available on the Xbox Store for just £6.99 / $7.99.

The MMA fighter and failed Irish presidential candidate had a small role in the 2016 shooter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Call of Duty doesn't have much luck with its stunt casting. Two years after Infinity Ward put Kevin Spacey in Advanced Warfare—before he was accused of sexual assault—it turned MMA fighter Conor McGregor into a future soldier, Captain Bradley Fillion, in Infinite Warfare.

McGregor's role was quite small, despite being one of the game's antagonists, and ended in his character's demise, but co-directors Jordan Hirsh and Taylor Kurosaki didn't want to cut any corners when it came to the mo-cap.

I got to work with Conor McGregor, and the story about Conor McGregor… We shot that in either 2015 or early 2016, but this is the height of him as a UFC fighter. And so of course I wanted him to do something really physical, to demonstrate how capable he is. He's shorter than me, but I was trying to explain to him the choreography that I wanted him to do at the beginning there, where he smashes the guy, and he grabbed me and flipped me onto the ground—very gently. And then did this punch [right in front of my face] that I could feel the wind from.

At the time, co-directors Hirsh and Kurosaki were trying to shake things up in regards to mo-cap. "I think that the folks at Infinity Ward probably thought I was a little crazy when I came in," Kurosaki tells us. "I think for every game they had done before that, you would maybe do some mocap or a cool takedown or a finisher, and then you'd have actors that would come into a VO booth and you'd have them come in one at a time and they'd read their lines and it’d be stitched together and then you're done. And they built a performance capture stage specifically for this project."

With Infinite Warfare, the team was doing full performance capture, so it needed its actors to get more physical.

Kurosaki remembers, after McGregor flipped him, that he "did this punch [right in front of my face] that I could feel the wind from. We're just rehearsing and figuring out the blocking. Everyone on the stage was, ‘Whoa, that was crazy! It was so fast!’ And of course, I had a different perspective than everyone else. Then everyone was laughing, and he helped me up, and I'm laughing. And then all of a sudden, this giant bead of sweat starts running down my face. I had this adrenaline, even though I knew I was perfectly safe. My body was just doing something that I couldn't control."

A few years later, McGregor started racking up criminal charges for assault. In 2019, he attacked a man for not accepting a drink in a Dublin pub. He pleaded guilty. In the same year, police in Ireland started investigating McGregor over allegations of multiple sexual assaults. He was not prosecuted, but a civil claim was made against him by Nikita Hand. In 2024, an Irish jury found that McGregor raped Hand.

Also in 2024, McGregor starred in Hitman, as one of its celebrity Elusive Targets—his second videogame role outside of the UFC games. IO Interactive stopped working with him after the ruling and removed him from the game as an Elusive Target.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Activision, unlike IO, left McGregor in the Infinite Warfare campaign. The fighter has not made any other videogame appearances since then. Prior to the ruling, he was a playable fighter in EA's UFC games, starting in 2014. He was the co-cover athlete in 2016's UFC 2 and the solo cover athlete in 2018's UFC 3. His last appearance in the series was in UFC 5 in 2023.

McGregor has had no scripted television cameos since 2024, appearing strictly as himself for promotional spots and interviews—including a guest appearance on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon in June 2026. Fallon and NBC were heavily criticised for inviting McGregor onto the show. He is also attached to host and executive-produce a Fox Nation competition series titled World's Baddest Man, slated for 2027.

#4034. "Keep talking about it": Raw Power Games call for Wishlist aid as they, and their historical strategy sandbox Chronicles: Medieval, lose funding

Raw Power Games, an independent studio comprising veteran developers of The Witcher 3, Total War: Three Kingdoms, and Crusader Kings III (among others), have called on players for support after losing their funding - an existential threat to both the organisation and to their debut, the still-in-development historical strategy game Chronicles: Medieval.

In a statement posted last week, Raw Power announced that "the necessary funding" behind the studio was no longer in place, despite Chronicles: Medieval – which was unveiled last year with an expensive-looking, Tom Hardy-narrated trailer – apparently being within touching distance of its planned early access launch. Hardy or no Hardy, however, the statement declared that they aren't "going down without a fight", hinting at talks with what could be possible new investors, asking interested would-be fans to "keep talking about" the game, and encouraging its inclusion on Steam Wishlists.

A few days on, the impact of this rallying call remains unclear. Raw Power Games have made no further statements, and Chronicles: Medieval does not seem to appear on Steam's own list of Top Wishlisted games. SteamDB have it at #26 in their desire-o-rankings, representing no change from its position immediately before the funding announcement was made, and while the game's Steam follower count has increased by over 1,000 week-on-week – significantly more so than surrounding games in the list – that doesn't feel like the kind of wild grassroots support that might save a dozens-strong studio.

Still, as my childhood television used to say, every little helps, and I'm inclined to hope for Raw Power's survival if only as an antidote to the enthusiasm-poisining dread of seeing so many other developers being laid off and shut down. Chronicles: Medieval looks promisingly ambitious too, mashing up sprawling Mount & Blade-style battles with an RPG-flavoured strategy layer that involves the player's custom-created character ascending the snooty social hierarchy of 14th century England. Best of luck to everyone trying to get it over the early access line.

#4033. Forza Horizon 6 Content Roadmap Revealed For Late 2026 & 2027

With a specific focus on January and February of next year

Ready for some more news on Forza Horizon 6? The team at Playground Games has announced a content roadmap for the game today, pulling the curtain back on their plans for the end of 2026 and all of next year.

You can get loads of detail about all of this in the video up above, but in a nutshell, we're getting Series 8 "Horizon Holidays" and Series 9 "Legendary Explorers" before the year is out. Then, as we head into January and February, Series 10 will be based around "Exotics and Tuners", while other new additions include a permanent new radio station, absolutely loads of new Reward Cars, and various other bits and bobs.

Most importantly, the first expansion for the game will also be released in January of 2027. Playground Games still doesn't want to talk about it just yet, but apparently we'll be hearing about it very soon.

News Forza Horizon 6's First Premium Expansion Planned For January 2027 Alongside PS5 Launch

Sony fans loved FH5, will they vibe with FH6? Probably

As you can see from the rest of this roadmap, the remainder of 2027 gets more vague for now, but it's confirmed that a second expansion is on the way along with a Festival Playlist overhaul, new race routes and various other new features.

They do talk quite a lot about the Festival Playlist overhaul in the video up above, so again, it's well worth a watch if you want to know more about what's on the way to Forza Horizon 6 in the future.

All of this sounds pretty good to us, and considering how the game has come in for a little bit of disgruntlement in recent months, it's clear to see that Playground Games is hoping for a strong 2027 when it comes to new FH6 content.

#4031. Fate of the Galaxy is a huge, fully-featured Star Wars space combat sim that, thanks to being a total conversion mod for Freespace Open, even runs on my rubbish laptop

Star Wars has been back in the news recently because, to cut a long story short, the US alt-right have decided that Darth Vader was actually the good guy. We are not here to indulge such buffoonery. We are here to talk about Fate of the Galaxy, a free unofficial space combat simulator set during the events of the original Star Wars trilogy, featuring several mission-based campaigns and a stable of Imperial and Rebel Alliance ships that ranges from the quad-blasting X-Wing to Boba Fett's Firespray 31. Also, Naboo starfighters, if you really must.

It's a total conversion of poor dead Volition's venerable dogfighter FreeSpace 2, running on the open source Free Space 2 Open engine via the popular Knossos launcher. You don't need a copy of FreeSpace 2 to play it. You also don't need to pay. And nor do you need a whizbang PC – this bucket of bolts hums along happily on my i5-1145G7 with no dedicated graphics card. As the Rancor said to the padawan: finally, some good food.

Fate of the Galaxy has been in development off and on for almost two decades, weathering a number of team changes and shifts of focus. The FreeSpace Wiki has a longer account of its travels. It's not an officially licensed Star Wars production, as made evident by a scrolling text intro which takes the official orchestral theme and moves every note up or down a place, as though spitefully jolting the piano around under John Williams' fingers. It's not quite as bizarre as Portsmouth Sinfonia's Also sprach Zarathustra but it did make me cackle like the Emperor contemplating a freshly made asteroid field. But then I began playing, and my presumptuous merriment became a frown of concentration.

While hardly Steel Battalion, Fate of the Galaxy is a proper nerdy sim with a bustling 3D cockpit and all sorts of keyboard shortcuts to try once and immediately forget. You'll need to funnel energy between fore and aft shields during bombing runs on Star Destroyers, target individual subsystems with your ion cannon, give orders to other pilots, and consider whether to synch different guns for maximum effect. I can run the game fine on my work laptop with integrated graphics, but I'm definitely feeling the need for a beefier keyboard. And also a joystick. Certainly, I'm not going to get far in LAN multiplayer with this hunk of junk.

It seems a very generous production, based on 30 minutes playing kiss-chase with TIE bombers. The story campaigns and quickfix stand-alone skirmishes aside, there's a mission editor with text-based files for easier sharing. There's also VR support with head-tracking, should you own one of those haunted helmets. Learn more via the online manual (Google Doc), and find Fate of the Galaxy itself on Moddb. You'll need around seven gigs of disc space.

This being the year 2026, there's the question of generative AI usage - a topic of much concern lately in modding circles. Fate of the Galaxy's official site boasts that all the visual assets were "made by humans only". I'm less sure about other aspects – there's seemingly some artificial VO during the tutorial, though it sounds like antiquated, less insidious robocaller software. The FreeSpace Open engine itself greatly pre-dates today's chatbot invasion. The original FreeSpace 2 launched in 1999 - a more civilised age, when everybody still thought Darth Vader was an arsehole.

#4029. Rimworld-inspired colony sim Stardeus gets a huge update representing a year's worth of expansion and revision, with new tools for evil AI overlords

"Stardeus is in an early stage in terms of bulk and complexity, but it's already a pleasant blend of interesting ideas that generate a mostly relaxing vibe," wrote gallant star captain.exe Sin Vega in our 2022 analysis of Rimworld-influenced colony manager Stardeus. "One to watch for sure." Well, let it not be said that we weren't watching.

Stardeus has received a gargantuan early access update that has been "a year in the making," according to developer Kodo Linija. It's still a game about being an AI running a badly damaged interstellar colony ship in top-down view – sending drones to restore the damage, before waking the quarrelsome human popsicles from their slumber. But the new version introduces a quest system and a new opening tutorial chain, the ability to form alliances with other starfaring factions, the possibility of lifelong injury due to failed surgery, and the timely option to become an evil AI and mind-control your crew with beta waves, amongst other dastardly antics.

It introduces a new interface and a new ship aesthetic, a trust system that governs the odds of a mutiny, and a revised colonist skill system. There's also a freshened-up ground combat element that's now built around "cover, suppression, stuns and fleeing", and a new approach to space battles that's all about managing Flux generated when you fire weapons or take shield damage. The update notes on Steam tote more than 1,500 changes, with the dev enthusing that there is "hardly a system in the game that wasn't rebuilt, reworked or expanded".

I confess, I hadn't heard of Stardeus before. It sounds like fun, in the Dwarf Fortressian sense. The 1.0 rollout is due in "approximately Q1 2027".

#4028. K-pop Royalty Recruited for PlayStation Korea's Glitzy GTA 6 Ad

One thing I always appreciate about PlayStation is its ability to appeal to localised audiences, despite its message being unified globally.

The company’s current marketing strategy revolves around GTA 6, and it’s using the slogan ‘Plays Best on PS5’. But it’s promoting this in a variety of ways around the world.

Its Korean commercial is particularly glitzy, featuring K-pop royalty like Jay Park and members from girl group QWER.

The cinematic trailer revolves around the 13-year wait since GTA 5.

In the video, the city lights go down and the aforementioned celebs all rush home to power up the game – on the PS5, of course.

It’s a fun ad, and it’s interesting to see Sony invest so much into a bespoke commercial like this.

It’s particularly amusing seeing as the Rockstar open world was almost denied release in South Korea, due to its inclusion of “out of context” nudity.

Of course, it’s targeted marketing like this that’s made PlayStation a powerhouse around the globe, and will help ensure GTA 6 sells best on Sony’s box by some margin.

#4027. PSA: Xbox And GTA 6 Have Both Pushed Out Small New Updates

One's a console update, the other potentially a "day one" patch

As we get ready to wrap up the working week here at Pure Xbox, we wanted to alert you to a couple of new updates that have been pushed out in recent days - one for Xbox consoles in general, and another specifically for GTA 6.

The Xbox console update was actually released on Wednesday, but nobody made a song and dance about it whatsoever, while the patch notes only referenced "general stability and performance improvements".

However, we now know that the update was related to the addition of achievements in four original Xbox games, and unless you download the update, you won't be able to see those achievements right now.

There's a chance your console may have downloaded this automatically but to check, go to "Settings", "System", "Updates" and then see if there's an update waiting to be downloaded or not.

News Four OG Xbox Games Are Getting Achievements For The First Time Ever

"We’re introducing one of the top requested features"

As for GTA 6, in addition to the 200GB+ preload that went live a few days ago, there's also now a new update as of a few hours ago that sits at around 2.2GB. You'll need to download this in order to start playing on November 19th.

Some people are speculating that this might be the so-called "day one patch", but who knows whether we might get another one between now and next Thursday. In any case, you'll want to get this queued up as soon as possible (unless you haven't installed the game yet, in which case it'll be included in your initial download).

There's a chance you may see a different size, but it's somewhere around that 2.2GB mark. We're also spotting that some people haven't got it yet for whatever reason, but it should roll out to all Xbox users in the very near future.

Don't forget that Alpha Skip-Ahead Xbox Insiders have also received a special new update this week that adds three new features for testing purposes, so if you're part of the Insider programme, keep an eye out for that.

We'll be back next week with loads more coverage on the GTA 6 launch, and here's hoping there are no more downloads to get us ready for November 19th. Just a few more sleeps until the big day!

Jensen Huang has resigned from his position as Nvidia CEO. That's such an odd sentence to write, as a huge part of my career as a tech journalist has revolved around covering Nvidia, its graphics cards, and its leather-jacketed chief.

As I write this article, I'm already seeing reactions on social media from PC gamers. Some are shocked, some are indifferent, and some appear to be celebrating. In terms of the latter, I'd imagine that's because the ex-Nvidia boss has become one of the most recognisable figures behind the great AI revolution, which, err, isn't popular within our hobby, to say the least.

Not only that, but RAM is ludicrously expensive, with storage not far behind. And graphics cards, Nvidia's gaming bread and butter? The price increases recently have been mind-boggling. All of these things are, in the main, AI server-demand induced, and Nvidia is behind the chips that power most of those servers, making vast amounts of money in the process.

And so on that level, I can understand why some might cheer his departure, equating the company's figurehead with Nvidia's new place in the AI economy as a whole—leaving us gamers in the lurch. But as far as I see it, Jensen Huang leaving the helm of Nvidia is unlikely to be a good thing for PC gaming.

I'll give you an unfortunate percentage: 7.4%. That's roughly how much of Nvidia's total revenue was brought in by gaming in the 2026 fiscal year. The company reported $193.7 billion in data center revenue. Its gaming division? $16 billion. That's despite the fact the company is estimated to hold 90% of the PC graphics card market share.

In terms of business fundamentals, Nvidia would be foolish to put more focus on gaming hardware while the AI cash cow continues to provide. Huang, however, still seemed reluctant to leave PC gaming entirely by the wayside during his tenure.

Those who have watched as many Nvidia GPU announcements as I have will know that walking on stage with a new graphics card, or gaming laptop, lit up Huang's face the most. 3D graphics was where the company began, after all, back when founders Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky, and Curtis Priem sat down at a Denny's in San Jose and put together a business plan. Or so the story goes.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

But now, someone new will be steering the ship. Colette Kress, the company's executive vice president and chief financial officer will serve as interim CEO, while the search begins for Huang's permanent replacement.

Whoever they are, they'll be taking over an absolute titan of tech, the behemoth standing behind the US position in the great AI race, and a company that will need to convince its investors that the AI good times are far from over. How big a factor do you think consumer graphics cards are likely to be in those discussions?

Personally, I reckon they're going to be pretty far down the list of priorities. Because this is big business, money talks, and AI data centers are where most of the cash still lies. I wish that wasn't true, but the figures speak for themselves.

So, if Nvidia pivots even further away from gaming hardware, where might your next graphics card come from? There's always AMD, who's CEO has recently proudly declared it as "a data center-first company." Hmm, I'm not too confident on the focus there, either. Or Intel, which... oh jeez, you too?

I'm not saying consumer gaming hardware, or Nvidia graphics cards, are going to disappear entirely in the face of the AI onslaught. But what I am saying is that, love him or loathe him, Jensen Huang was still an advocate for PC gaming—at least out of sentimentality, if nothing else.

He who became one of the primary movers of the AI market now threatening our hobby, was also an integral part of PC gaming's success. But now, Nvidia is likely to be making some big changes, sans Huang—and I find it hard to believe that many of them will be in our favour.

Andy built his first gaming PC at the tender age of 12, when IDE cables were a thing and high resolution wasn't. 26 years later (yes he's getting old), he now spends his days writing about and reviewing graphics cards, CPUs, keyboards, mice, gaming headsets and much, much more. You name it, if it's PC gaming hardware he'll write words about it, with opinions and everything.
