Asha Sharma doesn't specifically mention AI in her 25th anniversary message, but I'm pretty sure that's what she's talking about.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In a message marking the 25th anniversary of the first Xbox console, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma predicts that the future of gaming will look much like its beginning, "when a small team with a big idea could change how the world plays." And even though the term never actually appears in her post, yeah, I'm pretty sure she's talking about AI.

Sharma's message kicks off with a blast from the early days of Microsoft, beginning with a look at Microsoft Adventure, an adaptation of Colossal Cave "that looked more like MS-DOS than an early version of Minecraft," and the first-ever Microsoft staff photo that showcases some absolutely spectacular hair. From there it's a quick trip through Microsoft Flight Simulator, Quake, DirectX, and then in 2001, the original Xbox.

Naturally, there's a tribute to the "generations of employees, studios, developers, and partners" who helped create and grow Xbox, and the people who have played on various generations of consoles over the years.

"Since joining Xbox, I've heard stories of friendships that began over a session and lasted a lifetime, of people who met the person they would marry, and of parents now sharing the games they grew up on with their children," Sharma writes. "I've also heard about people who are no longer with us, and how much those hours spent playing together still mean to those who love them. Ultimately, this is why we exist."

From there, Sharma offers thoughts on the future of Xbox, and this is where I think it gets interesting: After comparing the size and capabilities of the original Microsoft Flight Simulator with the 2024 edition, she continues, "While modern games demonstrate the heights of human craft in ways unimaginable just decades ago, the cost, resources, and risk required to create them have grown just as dramatically. As a result, too many ideas never become games, and too many games fall short of what their creators imagined. For decades, this has been the unavoidable tradeoff of ambition. We must change this."

How exactly that change will come about goes unspecified, but my guess? She's talking about AI.

"Throughout human history, the scale of what we could create was determined by the people, capital, and resources we could command. That relationship is beginning to break," Sharma writes.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

"A single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations. A small team will be able to build worlds that today demand hundreds of developers and hundreds of millions of dollars. And our largest studios will be able to pursue ambitions as far beyond today’s games as Microsoft Flight Simulator 2024 is from its first entry in 1982."

The explosive rise in the cost of game development is undeniable. The pioneering open-world sci-fi RPG Starflight was literally made by five guys; its distant descendant Mass Effect: Andromeda credits 14 people for working on "audio design" alone. Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick summed up the situation quite aptly earlier this year, calling big-budget game development "a high-stakes game for big boys only"; the development budget of the upcoming Grand Theft Auto 6 is being talked about in terms of billions.

Despite Sharma's optimistic presentation, though, I'm not entirely confident that an AI-powered future where one person—or even a few—can do what currently takes hundreds is really a desirable outcome.

Alongside questions of ethics and artistic vision, there are also very pragmatic concerns about the long-term future of the games industry itself. Because really, the embrace of AI—not just at Xbox, but everywhere—is about cutting jobs. Bethesda had nine concept artists working on Starfield: What happens when somebody in an office decides they can get the same job done, pretty much, with two guys hammering out prompts? Maybe even just one? Quarterly profits and shareholder return may go up, but I doubt we'll be saying the same about the quality of the games we play.

Sharma concluded by writing that she believes "the future of gaming will look more like its beginning, when a small team with a big idea could change how the world plays." I would argue that small teams are already doing that—the big, billion-dollar blockbusters that have prompted these worries seem far more committed to merely giving us more of what we've already got.

The finale of the Final Fantasy 7 Remake trilogy dares to expand even further from its world to character customization

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you thought Final Fantasy 7 Revelation was going to rein things in after the maximalist scale of Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth, then think again. This is, after all, the finale of the Final Fantasy 7 Remake trilogy, so it's got to go out with a bang. Square Enix has also, so far, designed each instalment to be its own standalone RPG with a raft of new gameplay features rather than just a mere iteration of the next episode of the story.

While Final Fantasy 7 Revelation is already confirmed to be the largest entry to date – literally so with a file size estimated to be up to 200GB – there's plenty of new features that make this stand out from the already colossal achievements of its predecessors. This may still be a single-player story-driven party-based action RPG set over a planet-sized open world, but the developers have cooked up a lot more that demonstrates why it wasn't just called Final Fantasy 7 Remake Part 3.

There's potentially still more that Square Enix will reveal as the finale's April 8 launch date approaches, but from our hands-on time and official announcements made so far, these are the eight new features coming to Final Fantasy 7 Revelation that we feel is going to make this the most definitive of all the remake releases to date.

With the remake trilogy drawing to a close early 2027, we get ready for the epic conclusion with our Final Fantasy 7 Revelation Big Preview across hands-on impressions, dev access, and deep dives into the whole adventure so far.

Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth had already given us the impossible with an open world that really does encompass a world, and while Final Fantasy 7 Revelation adds to that with still several more locations, including Mideel and Wutai, its planetary scale has been magnified with verticality. You're not just fast-traveling to locations, but you have Cid's airship, the Highwind, which you can use to fly over any location and then jump out and parachute down seamlessly in real-time.

It's already a huge change from the original game where you could only access part of the overworld if you had enough space to land the Highwind. Instead of just warping to a set checkpoint, it also means if there's a nearby side quest marker, you can glide that way directly, or there might be another secret at a higher elevation you hadn't noticed before that's worth trying to land at to investigate. It's certainly a way to make revisiting places feel fresh again in Final Fantasy 7 Revelation.

While Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth had a new chocobo for each region, Final Fantasy 7 Revelation reunites you with yellow-feathered chocobo Piko from the Grasslands, this time as your sole mount. That might sound like something this instalment is reining in, but what it actually means is Piko will feel like a permanent addition to the party. Not just a mount for getting you from A to B, they'll actually level up and can even fight alongside you in battle.

Old-school fans may lament that there won't be chocobo-breeding like the original game, but I think having Piko grow and unlock new abilities, both in terms of traversal and combat, during your journey makes for a more meaningful companion than any other gaming mount. It's not like The Witcher 3's Roach was ever useful in a fight.

Sign up to our Switch 2 Spotlight newsletter to make sure you get the very latest news on Nintendo's new console and its games every week

Although Cid Highwind and Vincent Valentine were introduced in Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth, they become fully playable party members in Final Fantasy 7 Revelation. While it will be exciting getting to grips with Cid's dragoon-style fighting style or Vincent's Galian beast transformation, you'll also be able to select them or any of the other party members as the playable character during exploration.

Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth did also try to mix things up occasionally in dungeons where the party would get split up or put you in control of a certain character in story-specific missions. Nonetheless, this small but meaningful change means you can spend more time controlling your favorite character while out in the wider world. It also makes sense given the story will cover the section when central protagonist Cloud will be out of action. And if you play as Vincent, it might be the closest we'll get to a Dirge of Cerberus remaster – it could still happen, right?

Arguably the most significant new feature in Final Fantasy 7 Revelation is the FITS (Function-Integrated Tactical Suitwear) system, which may also sound rather similar to Dresspheres for any Final Fantasy 10-2 fans. Essentially, you can give each party member new threads or armor that also give them new classes that recall classic Final Fantasy jobs, such as Knight, Black Mage, or Summoner.

There's real style to this too as each outfit is tailored to each character rather than wearing the same job uniform. The abilities that come with each outfit are also actually additions rather than changing your class entirely, so if Tifa is dressed as a white mage, rest assured you can still kick ass with her divekick as before. That also means, if you're not looking to think too deeply about builds and just like the outfits as a cosmetic, then that's totally viable too.

The Black Materia is going to be a crucial plot point in Final Fantasy 7 Revelation, as it's what allows Sephiroth to summon Meteor, and its ominous presence in the sky is going to be inescapable as you play through the game. Its activation will however also cause significant change to the world, notably the emergence of Weapons roaming the world.

Perhaps more significant is how the effects of Black Materia may alter the world's terrain. We can only speculate at this point what that can mean, but taking the addition of the Highwind and Piko into account as new ways of traversal, don't be surprised if the Grasslands suddenly has new structures or a rupture in the ground that require more verticality in traversal to explore. Call it the Tears of the Kingdom effect, but it should also mean you aren't just going back to explore the exact same regions as you left them in Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth.

Equipping Materia to use spells or gain buffs remains a key aspect of Final Fantasy 7 Revelation, though being treated as its own standalone game, I won't be surprised if that means having to upgrade them and find new Materia again, even if you might start with a default number of them as with Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth.

But, one area this finale plans to go further is how many Materia you can potentially link together. While we have already had gear that could link two Materia together, there may also be armor that can link three Materia together. That could mean being able to Magnify Materia to two separate spells so that they both reap the benefits, or potentially other uses that I'm still racking my brain over.

Synergy was a cool feature introduced in Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth where you can have two party members team up together in battle. These ranged from real-time Synergy Skills like Aerith calling another party member to be her bodyguard or Tifa getting someone to launch her towards an enemy, to Synergy Abilities as show-stopping as Limit Breaks. How do you top that? Triple Synergy!

Given the three-person party size that was also true of the original game, it seems such a logical conclusion to have them all unite in one killer combo. That said, given the complexity of coordinating three characters simultaneously, I suspect this may just be limited to an ultimate ability that may only be available in specific situations, but expect them to leave a lasting impression.

Players looking for a proper challenge in Final Fantasy 7 Revelation don't need to finish the game to unlock a hard mode. Given how long this finale is going to be, that's already a tall order. But it also doesn't mean it's going to be hard mode available from the start but with that mode's item restrictions or enemies with double the health as with past games.

What it actually means in Final Fantasy 7 Revelation is that because of the huge amount of side quests available and freedom to explore from very early on, there is absolutely nothing stopping you from taking on the toughest side quests and bosses even if you've vastly underleveled, while there are of course also the Weapons roaming the land, just tempting you to go pick a fight, whether or not you're ready.

#3898. God of War Laufey delayed three months to May 2027, as Sony Santa Monica escapes a packed February

"We will make the most of each moment until then."

God of War Laufey has been delayed. Sony Santa Monica's PS5 exclusive is now dodging the crowded month of February and will instead come out on 20th May, 2027.

Developer Sony Santa Monica announced it's pushing back the upcoming action epic via a brief social media post. While the studio stopped short of giving a reason for the delay, it did say it's using the extra time to polish Faye's solo adventure.

"Since the reveal of God of War Laufey in June, we've been deeply grateful to see so much excitement for Faye's journey through the Everywhen. We don't take for granted the trust placed in the studio to make an extraordinary experience worthy of the passion and dedication of our fans," the studio wrote.

"With this in mind, we've made the decision to delay God of War Laufey's release to May 20th, 2027," the statement continued. "We will make the most of each moment until then by putting in the finishing touches and pushing the game to its fullest potential. On behalf of everyone on the team, we appreciate your patience and we'll be back to share more updates soon."

God of War Laufey is notably the first game in the famed PlayStation series to not star Kratos in the lead role. This time around, Faye takes the lead through a version of the afterlife that houses gods and deities from multiple mythologies - and it's bringing back the original series' faster combat, too.

Of course, Kratos will return in future God of War games (he also shows up here and there during Faye's romp), and whatever that next Kratos game becomes, it'll supposedly connect to the events of Laufey, according to the developer.

On the bright side, the delay might be good news for anyone worried about their impossibly large and ever expanding backlogs. February 2027 is already packed with really exciting games - from the Fable reboot and Persona 4 Revival to Metro 2039. Hopefully, Laufey's delay gives everyone more breathing room.

#3897. Bandai Namco is liquidating Unknown 9: Awakening studio Reflector Entertainment, following multiple previous layoffs since the game's launch

As another addition to the slew of smaller studios being dissolved by their parent companies, Bandai Namco announced in a press release that they are shutting down their subsidiary studio Reflector Entertainment, a Montreal studio responsible for 2024's action-adventure game Unknown 9: Awakening. In its notice, Bandai Namco explains that the reason for the liquidation is due to Reflector not meeting its expectations for "future business plans, necessary additional investment, and the possibility of profitability and business continuation."

The press release notes that the liquidation of Reflector will result in an estimated "extraordinary loss" of around 21 million euros, or 3.5 billion yen, for Bandai Namco in its Q3 fiscal report of this year. This is not the first time Reflector has been cut by Bandai, as around a month after the launch of Unknown 9: Awakening and presumably in response to its low sales, 18% of the workforce was laid off. 2025 then saw further redundancies amidst the cancellation of a prospective project, though details on those layoffs were not granted by the company. Unknown 9 was intended to be a transmedia franchise involving the game as well as comic books and novels, but these ambitions never came to pass.

Bandai Namco notes that the liquidation will be held to local laws and procedures, which make the actual schedule of the process uncertain for now. A similar process faces Arkane Lyon, which is currently in a purgatory of having been chosen for closure by Microsoft, but temporarily protected by French labor laws that prevent it from being suddenly closed without proper negotiation and procedure.

Michael B. Jordan’s Thomas Crown Affair is going to light up the early part of the 2027 movie schedule, and the full trailer has finally dropped after we got a teaser a few months ago. Even though I expected Jordan to look as cool as he’s ever looked in that one, my expectations were exceeded by the trailer. I love the ‘90s version of the movie with Pierce Brosnan and Renee Russo, but Jordan and Adria Arjona look even sexier, if that’s even possible. The movie is definitely bringing the heat.

That’s before we even get to the action. In the trailer, we see Jordan (who is also directing the movie) climbing buildings, racing cars, and, of course, stealing art. We also get a little glimpse into Kenneth Branagh’s character as a rival to Thomas’ Crown, and it looks like there will be quite the confrontation between the two. While Thomas is playing Crown, and Arjona is clearly playing the role of the woman chasing him for stolen art (Russo’s character in the earlier film and Faye Dunaway’s character in the original version starring Steve McQueen), Branagh’s looks new, and I think it already looks like a great dynamic.

It’s one of the most stylish trailers I’ve seen in a long time. Add in music from Jon Baptiste, and we might just have the sexiest movie of the year to keep us warm this winter. I’ve been counting down the months and weeks for this one, and March 5th still can’t come soon enough!

#3895. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's Navi actor reprises her role after 28 years, but it was a total accident due to Nintendo's blind auditions

For The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's shiny new remake, Nintendo unintentionally cast the same actor twice - 28 years apart - to deliver Navi's infamous "Heys!" and "Listens!"

The Switch 2's Ocarina of Time makes a pretty substantial change to the N64's Ocarina of Time, released almost three decades prior. There's proper voice acting this time, of course - not just grunts and murmurs and hyahs. But even when retroactively adding new things, Nintendo wanted to ensure the remake's cast matched the original's pretty faithfully, so the developer held blind auditions that eventually paved the way for one actor to reprise their role during Link's adventure.

"We felt that if we were going to improve the graphics so dramatically, the cutscenes needed to be fully voiced to match," director HokWai Ng explained in the most recent Ask The Developer blog. "But at the same time, we knew we shouldn't mess with established perceptions of how certain characters sound based on the original. Navi's "Listen!" is one example. Even someone who's never played The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time may have heard it before. We absolutely didn't want to change anything as iconic as that."

To maintain the original's nostalgic sounds and voices, Nintendo held blind auditions with the goal of finding actors who could recreate the "feel of the original game."

Series director Eiji Aonuma recalls that the team wanted to choose actors "based solely on which voices most closely resembled those of the original." And, who woulda guessed? "As fate would have it, one of the actors we selected had actually voiced the same character in the Nintendo 64 version. None of us saw that coming."

The duo didn't outright name which character they're talking about, but fans have long been speculating that Kaori Mizuhashi might be reprising her role as Link's trusty fairy companion Navi - at least, in the Japanese language version. A leaked online video of the game's credits now also confirms that Mizuhashi is back almost three decades later. I suppose it only makes sense that the person who most closely resembles Navi is Navi.

Chris Donlan called the new version an "astonishing remake" in his five-star Eurogamer Ocarina of Time review.

#3894. Company of Heroes 3 developer admits "it was a lot" to make the 3.0 overhaul patch alongside regular updates, singleplayer DLC, and a whole spinoff game

The Company of Heroes 3's 3.0 update is huge. Touching virtually every part of the three-year-old RTS, the patch notes are longer than, well, my arm isn't a great measure of patch note length. Let's just say the headline features of overhauled VFX and audio don't really cover it. It also comes with new autumn and winter biomes, an updated grand strategy campaign, improvements to unit AI, and a whole host of other changes.

Talking to Relic ahead of the 3.0 update's launch I learned a little more about the scale of work that went on behind the scenes to make it happen, but also a little more about why Relic are still supporting the game three years after it was released and two years after separating from Sega.

The team began planning the 3.0 update two years ago, seeing the series' 20th anniversary as an opportunity to make a significant update to Company of Heroes 3, and focus on issues players had flagged since launch. "The VFX were called out," executive producer Denise Christie tells me. "Same thing with a lot of our audio."

Relic were already releasing patches every three months, but the changes they were looking at were much too large for those smaller updates. If they had tried to do the work as part of the small updates, approaching the problems with piecemeal solutions, it would have turned Company of Heroes 3 into a hodgepodge of new and old assets. "We wanted to make sure it was a cohesive package," principal designer Eric Wrobel says. "If you increase the quality of one thing, you have to do it equally across so much stuff." Otherwise you end up with "One that looks awesome and one that's like, 'Oh, this one's kind of gross'."

Complicating matters, though, was that the team couldn't down tools and focus on just these large changes. As well as the small patches that were still going out every three months, both the VFX and audio teams were also contributing the battlegroup DLC packs which added new units to the game. "They would work on stuff and in one branch that was the 3.0 work and then they would go ahead and do some battlegroup stuff and come back to that," Christie says. "It was a lot."

As the 3.0 update grew in scope, it also meant other departments were contributing to the anniversary release while working on the smaller updates and DLC. "For us to create future maps for Company of Heroes 3, we were going to have an issue that our assets were getting stale," Christie explains. So, as part of 3.0, Relic's art department created autumn and winter asset packs, as well as a new Industrial theme. This then created more work for the VFX team, who have added rain and snow, as well as a transition effect showing soil and concrete moving from dry to wet.

Not to be outdone, the design team also made significant changes to the singleplayer Italy campaign. The towns that dot the dynamic grand strategy-inspired map now have individual upgrades, making for more meaningful decisions when it comes to which settlement you capture next. And, responding to one of the main criticisms of Company of Heroes 3's singleplayer, they also updated the computer's AI so it makes smarter decisions in both the turn-based and real-time battles. "We wanted to get this feel like there was that sort of back and forth of the AI resisting you and pushing forward into your territory and actually taking your stuff, which wasn't really happening in any of the previous updates," Wrobel says.

Further complicating matters was the fact that alongside these regular updates, the DLC, and the big 3.0 update release work, was that Relic also released Final Stand in July, a roguelike horde mode spinoff of Company of Heroes 3. "We had to be very careful not to accidentally introduce this 3.0 work that was also happening at the same time," Christie says." The improvements in this update have also rolled out for the spinoff, too.

Naturally, Relic aren't doing all this work purely out of the goodness of the hearts. The regular updates keep players engaged, Christie explains, and "hopefully bring back lapsed players who were frustrated by some of these things." It's something the team have already seen happen before, Wrobel explains. "We saw with the 2.0 update that we had a big spike of users and that was great, but because that improved the overall quality of the game, we saw each month we were selling more copies than we were before. People have been buying these games for years and years and years, so if we invest in this now we're going to see returns for quite a long time into the future as well."

"If we were starting to see that tail down then we probably would have made a very different decision to be honest, but that's not what we see," Christie adds.

The next release for Company of Heroes 3 is a singleplayer DLC, Operation Torch, due out on November 25th. (So, if you're keeping count, that was also in the works while the update, battlegroup DLC, and spinoff were all being made.) Until now, Relic's additions to the RTS have been focused on the multiplayer community, adding new units to be used online or in offline skirmishes. Operation Torch brings new scripted missions that trace a set of soldiers moving through North Africa.

After that, though, I ask if Relic plans to continue adding to Company of Heroes 3 or if they're ready to move onto a new project. "Well, it's both actually," CEO Justin Dowdeswell tells me. "We would love to continue with Company of Heroes 3 and not solely as a place for us to experiment. That's one of the advantages of being smaller, and being able to make decisions. We're not going to leave Company of Heroes 3. It's an and function. We are going to embark on the next thing."

So, it doesn't sound like Relic are taking anything off their plate…

Demon Slayer may be rounding out its movie trilogy over the next few years, but Aniplex chairman Atsuhiro Iwakami is thinking much further afield.

Speaking to Bloomberg (via ScreenRant), Iwakami said he aims for Demon Slayer to endure as a franchise for up to another century, perhaps much in the same way Disney, Star Wars, and Marvel have enraptured audiences across the decades.

"With Demon Slayer, it is our intent to make this last 10 or 20, if not 50 to 100 years," Iwakami said. "We want to make sure we’re part of creating the type of franchise that can withstand decades."

Tanjiro's story may have already come to a close in the pages of the manga (and will be wrapped up in the third Demon Slayer Infinity Castle film, likely before 2030), but that doesn't mean it has to end there. With Hashira aplenty through the years – and a demon scourge not likely to go anywhere – the series feels rich for mining spin-offs and side stories in much the same way the likes of Dragon Ball has done since the 1980s.

In the more immediate term, the wait goes on for Demon Slayer Infinity Castle 2. Crunchyroll CEO Rahul Purini told GamesRadar+ in May that it is "actively in production." Since then, no announcement has been forthcoming – though December's Jump Festa event could be the destination for those hoping for a sequel release date.

Beyond that, who knows? But Demon Slayer could be around for a very, very long time to come.

For more, we have a guide to the rest of 2026's new anime, plus a look at how to watch Demon Slayer in order. Just to get a head start on the next few decades.

#3892. Arkane union says closing the studio "would probably be more expensive" for Xbox than simply finishing Marvel's Blade

"Microsoft based its decision only on stone cold and inhuman logic."

Xbox would probably spend more money shutting down Arkane Lyon than it would trying to finish and release Marvel's Blade, according to a union representing workers from the beloved imsim studio.

In a statement posted to the STJV (Syndicat des travailleureuses du jeu vidéo) website, the French union claimed that development on Marvel's Blade is "going fine" and is shaping up to be on par with Arkane's widely acclaimed gameography. By choosing to part ways with and potentially close the famed studio, the union says Microsoft is "sabotaging the game it funded."

After Xbox's sweeping job cuts and divestments from several first-party studios, Arkane was recently given until December to find a new buyer and ensure its future. Ubisoft Entertainment (Assassin's Creed, Rainbow Six) is reportedly one of the companies interested in buying the studio behind Dishonored, Prey and the upcoming superhero adaptation, though nothing has been finalised yet.

The union also blamed many of the studio's problems on Microsoft - a hiring freeze that lasted more than a year supposedly inflated the game's budget and caused additional internal delays. "Microsoft now use those same delay and additional costs as a reason to close the studio," the statement said.

"Even this closure itself is done against any financial logic, as closing Arkane today would probably be more expensive than finishing the game," it continued. "The truth is that Microsoft based its decision only on stone cold and inhuman logic, in which our lives, projects and dreams are voided, so we can better serve Microsoft's short term financial goals[...] The decision to close Arkane is solely the brutal application of a never-ending search for maximum profit optimization. Arkane is profitable. Just not profitable for Microsoft."

The union's list of demands now asks for employees to be able to have a say in choosing a potential buyer, as well as protections against any layoffs that might happen in the next few years. Should acquisition talks fail, the union claimed that the resources in Microsoft's redundancy package are "outrageously low" - so it's also demanding a redundancy payment of €200,000 per employee and further support.

Arkane's not the only developer reeling from Xbox's cuts. Double Fine (Psychonauts), Compulsion Games (South of Midnight) and Undead Labs (State of Decay) all managed to buy their independence, but had to lay off some staff as a result. It's not looking good for Hellblade developer Ninja Theory, either.

#3891. Nvidia shareholders have filed a lawsuit against the tech company over claims that they were misled regarding CEO Jensen Huang's affair

If I wasn't so sick of hearing about AI every day of my life at the moment I might have found it funny to hear that one of the biggest peddlers of the poison around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was caught having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Oh who am I kidding, it is funny! And despite knowing that this won't likely push Nvidia away from AI, I am a bit tickled to hear that the tech company and Huang are on the receiving end of a lawsuit.

The suit in question, as reported by The Guardian, is based on a complaint filed in California's federal court on behalf of Mark Kistenmacher by Rosen Law Firm. Kistenmacher is an Nvidia shareholder, and with this suit he's seeking to "recover compensable damages," for himself and other shareholders due to the "precipitous decline in the market value of the Company’s securities." What a palaver! I do not imagine this will be resolved particularly quickly.

As it currently stands, Huang has only admitted to having an affair rather than any trade secrets being leaked anywhere. Nvidia had this to say on the matter: "While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information. Jensen fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it. The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate."

The concern comes from the person Huang had an affair with, one Alice Huang (no, they aren't related), a former managing director of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre company who have allegedly given Chinese companies Nvidia chips they bought billions of US dollars of. A messy situation to be sure, and one I unconfidently hope brings about the end of AI, somehow.

GTA 6 required a total of three ratings reviews by South Korea's GCRB—and Cyberleek might have had something to do with it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Grand Theft Auto 6 has been granted an Adults Only rating in South Korea by the country's Game Content Rating Board. But in the weeks preceding that decision, the board had nearly refused to issue the game an age rating—effectively leaving it ineligible for sale in South Korea—due to ratings officials' concerns that GTA 6 might be way too comfortable hanging unprompted hog.

According to GCRB meeting minutes obtained by South Korean outlet Inven (via Kotaku), GTA 6 required a total of three ratings reviews, in which committee members repeatedly debated the presence of what they described as "out-of-context genital nudity"—a perception that seemed to have been informed by the leaked GTA 6 developer build footage circulated by cryptopeddling cornball master criminal, Cyberleek.

The GCRB's initial rating review for GTA 6 took place on September 10, during which committee members argued over whether the game's "out-of-context genital nudity" was grounds for refusal. Previously, the GCRB's rating standards automatically rejected games with exposed genitalia, but those standards were relaxed in 2025 to permit an Adults Only rating for "cases where suggestive bodily exposure is directly and specifically depicted," as long as that depiction didn't extend to graphic sexual acts.

Despite that revision, the committee members arguing to refuse an age rating for GTA 6 said that, while the GCRB had previously permitted "a certain degree of genital exposure where there is narrative justification," they "did not believe genital exposure to this extent falls within acceptable limits."

As the report notes, that first review meeting occurred before the GCRB received a playable GTA 6 build, meaning that the GCRB members' perception of the extent of visible in-game genitalia could have been informed by Cyberleek's leaked footage of an in-game nudist colony—an area that, despite the abundance of human flesh on display, didn't actually entail much sex going on. It was mostly just nude people standing around doing people things.

The GCRB committee members in favor of an Adults Only rating noted as much, saying that "in this game, scenes with heavy exposure are not particularly sexual," while "conversely, in sexual scenes, exposure is limited." The first meeting ended in a 3-3 tie vote, leading the committee to postpone its decision and instead recommend to Rockstar that the game be modified.

The GCRB did eventually receive a playable build of GTA 6 on September 28—just six days before its scheduled second review meeting on October 2. While an initial report from its gameplay researcher indicated that "genital exposure scenes mostly appeared as one-off mission backgrounds and did not lead to sexual interactions," the committee decided to once again postpone its decision simply because the game was too damn huge for it to be confident that it had seen all the relevant cases of penises and/or vulvas in the wild.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

A few on the committee remained skeptical, however: "The basic principle of rating refusal applies when bodily exposure of sexual acts are depicted explicitly or excessively so as to disrupt social order," one GCRB committee member said. "By that standard, the current bodily exposure is sufficiently explicit and excessive."

In its third and final review meeting on October 16, the GCRB—informed in part by the fact that 10 other institutions like the US's ESRB and Europe's PEGI had issued their own ratings—ultimately voted 8-1 in favor of granting GTA 6 an Adults Only rating. Its researchers concluded that, after playing the game more thoroughly, scenes featuring full-frontal nudity didn't allow for any sexual interaction, and that cutscene sequences where protagonists Jason and Lucia did do sex at each other didn't expose any genitalia.

Interestingly, the GCRB researchers also confirmed that they couldn't replicate the ability to fully strip Jason and Lucia of their clothes that was shown in Cyberleek videos, inadvertently confirming that the GTA 6 build that'll be available to the public won't allow players to roam Vice City in the nude. Apologies if you were particularly invested in seeing Jason's dong.

And additional apologies to the one dissenting GCRB member who still voted for refusing an age rating for GTA 6, in part due to their fear that the rating could serve as precedent for other genres, meaning "background genital exposure will frequently appear in future RPGs as a result." I suspect they're going to have a rough time once Divinity comes out.

#3889. Valve explains why it's running behind on Steam game approvals, asks developers to perform basic release checks to prevent re-reviews

In the wake of witnessing an unprecedented number of game submissions to Steam over the last few months, Valve has been forced to delay approvals in order to deal with the existing backlog.

Following complaints by game developers on social media and elsewhere, Valve has now responded to explain why it's taking longer to get games approved. The short version: re-reviews are clogging up the system.

"We aim to test every game build in a timely manner, typically within three-five business days," Valve wrote in a Steam post. "However, we're running a little behind right now and taking up to 12 business days. Much of that delay is due to having to re-review games, which isn't great for you or for us."

As Valve explained in the post, games need to be re-reviewed when they're rejected for missing key quality assurance checks. In an effort to make it easier for developers to get it right the first time, Valve updated the Steam release checklist to include new, tighter requirements.

These include a requirement to run the game through Steam for at least five minutes. According to Valve, some of the games submitted have not been played through Steam.

"This means that even if a game runs smoothly when a dev launches their executable directly, they might have missed basic steps that would impact a user installing and playing via Steam," Valve explained.

Valve is also making it a rule to mention whether the game requires common redistributables such as DirectX, Visual C++, .NET, XNA. While Steam can automatically install many common redistributables, it needs to know which ones are needed (if any). There are also new rules about achievement readiness, cloud save detection, and some updates to Steam store page requirements.

"We now surface some of the most common issues we see missed, along with asking for some information to help our reviewers from the start," Valve added. "For example, if your game offers multiple languages and you've indicated that on your store page, we'll ask you to ensure you've included them in your build".

While Valve did not directly name gen-AI as a potential reason for this rise in the number of poor submissions, it's clear the Steam company needs to find a way to deal with the massive number of AI-assisted games.

Valve recently addressed Steam's AI game cloning problem by suggesting developers make their games less copyable. Incidentally, some of the developers whose game approvals are delayed now fear their games will be cloned by others using gen-AI and land a Steam page before the original article has made it out of submission.

Actor Anthony Clark, star of the early 2000s CBS sitcom Yes, Dear, has passed away. Co-star and actor Mike O'Malley shared the news, as he paid tribute to Clark and talked about the friendship they had before they ever worked together on television. He also opened up about the last phone call he had with the late actor.

O'Malley, who recently appeared on the 2026 TV schedule via a guest spot on NCIS, said a few words about Clark on X. He made audiences laugh as Greg, who often played the straight man to the sillier antics of his friend Jimmy. O'Malley talked about how he first met Clark, and how they'd only just recently spoken before his death:

Anthony Clark died yesterday. He was a hilarious guy. When my wife Lisa and I were dating back in the mid-nineties, Anthony was already famous in Boston, regularly selling out comedy shows. The first time we saw him at The Comedy Connection we laughed and laughed and laughed. He was so unique—one of those comics who is laughing along with you at the absurdity of his stories and observations. I was a fan before I was a friend. We spoke on the phone three weeks ago. He had us laughing loudly once again. Attached are some snapshots from our last episode of 'Yes Dear' which ended twenty years ago after 122 episodes. Rest in peace. Tony.

While Yes, Dear isn't available with a Paramount+ subscription or on other platforms, it was a successful CBS comedy in its day, with a six-season run. Greg and Jimmy's families represented two different households and the vastly different ways they raised their children, despite their long friendship.

32 Underrated TV Shows From The '90s That Don't Get Talked About Much These Days

Mike O'Malley has continued his acting career with more appearances on sitcoms, including memorable stints on My Name Is Earl and Glee. As for Anthony Clark, he had a brief hosting stint on Last Comic Standing, but ultimately stepped away from Hollywood and lived a quiet life.

As for the cause of death, Deadline reported that Anthony Clark passed following complications from pneumonia. O'Malley did not make mention of the illness in his tribute, and it is not known how long the former actor struggled from the sickness.

While Clark was known to many as a television star, his start came in stand-up comedy. He was famously featured in a 1995 HBO special in which he starred alongside Dave Chappelle, Dave Attell, and Louis C.K.

After the special, he secured a few film roles, including the barber seen in Sean Connery's The Rock. I was also reminded while looking at his filmography that he was in the drama Paid in Full, as well as River Phoenix's The Thing Called Love. His final film appearance would be in the 2011 comedy My Uncle Rafael, which starred John Michael Higgins.

He had a recurring guest role on Ellen, too, which ultimately paved the way for his leading role on Yes, Dear. I'm a little shocked to see it isn't available on streaming, and I would love to check out one of the best sitcoms of the 2000s again in light of this news.

CinemaBlend offers its condolences to the family and friends of Anthony Clark, and wishes them well during this time. Here's hoping for more tributes from those around Hollywood and stand-up comedy who knew him, and more stories about his life.

The previously promised social space will be coming with this update too, and it's called Limbo. Morbidly appropriate! You can hang out here with your buds, head to a mini arena for some impromptu matches (I think), or head to the firing range where you can test out your weapons. You'll also be able to try out the new runner shell, Bishop, a cooler than you, samurai-sword-wielding robot who can jump real good and do that cool movie thing where it slices a whole bunch of enemies at once in one swing real quick like.

What will undoubtedly have some folks going "Halo's back!" is the beginning of a beta test for a team deathmatch mode. The Halo comparison is apt not simply because of the fact that it's Bungie who are making it, but because there's a deep-voiced announcer guy talking about all the sick kills you do. Details are slim on how this will work too. Beyond that, there's a few new weapons to flaunt, and maybe most excitingly, big ole alien enemies to take on.

You've still got a little while to wait for Symbiosis, which is currently slated to launch on December 8th. The game will be free to play from then until December 15th, too, obviously in a bid to show sceptics how good it is now (hopefully it is good, for Bungie's sake).

#3886. Despite hardware worries and rising costs, Sony says PlayStation 6 development is on track and "progressing as scheduled"

Today, Thursday 5th November, 2026, Sony shared its latest financial results, reporting on the second quarter of financial year 2026 for the company. In a wide-ranging set of statements, we learned that the company's overall profits have been charged by the box office success of Spider-Man: Brand New Day, and that its annual profit outlook has been raised following a particularly successful quarter.

As for PlayStation, Sony CFO Lin Tao hinted at the status of the PlayStation 6 - not yet named as such - which is currently being worked on in the company's gaming division. She noted that the console is "progressing as scheduled" and that staff are making "solid progress" on the machine (thanks, VGC). Tao also revealed that it's been a strong year for the PS5; total sales for the console have reached 97.9 million, thanks to a further 2.6 million sales throughout July, August and September 2026.

The most interesting bytes of information teased out of this call relate to Tao's claim that Sony has been able to offset the rise in memory costs via cost reductions and price increases, all helped by a yearly operating income boost of 89 percent. Sony notes that it has secured enough memory hardware for its next business year, which helps prepare the ground for PlayStation 6 production which should kick off in earnest next year.

"Although new PS5 unit sales are gradually declining as expected at this stage of the console life cycle, the PlayStation platform continues to expand and grow in a stable manner," Tao explained. "[Next year,] we intend to make solid progress in preparing for the next-generation platform."

Tao outlines that Sony is beginning to pivot towards this new platform in terms of both investment and production, and that Sony will "attach great importance to a new platform and make the necessary investments for that." This platform - the as-yet-unofficially-named PS6 - will be announced "at an appropriate time in the future".

This all follows reports that the PS6's memory and storage alone reportedly cost more than $680, and that there is still no hard release date set for the console. In light of the fact that console manufacturing is being heavily impacted by the on-going component shortage, many are expecting the price of the base PS6 to be over $1000. We will have to see what Sony announces over the next year before we know for certain.

#3885. Ahead of GTA 6 and as concerns over genAI PC ports grow, Take-Two's CEO says they're revving up their "technical defences" and "legal activites" over piracy

"[Piracy is] going to become more of a challenge… and we're aware of that"

It's a bit of a time for AI and games at the moment, 'ey? A bad time, obviously, as it's infecting everything from game development, to the modding community, to native PC ports of a remake of a very popular game that I won't link to for fear of a certain company finding out where I live and ending me there and then. And of course, the latter may be a concern for one Rockstar Games and the impending release of GTA 6. But according to Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick, game's publisher, they are currently technically and legally preparing themselves.

IGN recently spoke to Zelnick regarding potential AI cloning concerns, notably about any business issues they may face as a result. "I don't think it’s a financial matter, in terms of a threat to our business," Zelnick explained. "I do think it’s a creative matter. It's important to everyone, our developers and our consumers alike, to deliver the experience Rockstar envisions. And at the same time, of course, we protect our intellectual property vigilantly. So we are focused on these concerns. We're not in the least cavalier about them. Technology is advancing quickly. And at the same time, I do think that pretty much everyone wants the Rockstar experience as Rockstar intended."

Zelnick also made a comment about thinking "all companies should be protecting intellectual property, their own and everyone else's," in response to a question about whether he wants to see OpenAI follow in Claude's footsteps by limiting the potential for genAI clones. "If you're in the intellectual property business, which Anthropic is and OpenAI is, then it seems ironic on the one hand to stomp on someone else's IP and hope that yours is protected," he said.

It was during an investor Q&A where Zelnick dug into the precautions Take-Two are take-twoing in regards to the growing threat of AI. "[Piracy is] going to become more of a challenge… and we're aware of that. So we are utterly focused on enhancing our technical defenses and enhancing our legal activities appropriately. And at the same time, without in any way being cavalier, every entertainment business that exists is subject to some element of piracy. So this is likely to invade our business to a greater or lesser extent. I think it will be manageable and we are focused on it."

Essentially: unless you want to face the wrath of the kinds of lawyers multi-billion dollar companies can afford, I wouldn't bother trying to clone GTA 6 with AI! Probably won't end well!

#3884. World of Warcraft: Forever is off to a great start with Blizzard's smoothest launch in memory

World of Warcraft: Forever came out last night. Those who stayed up were prepared for the usual from major WoW releases: long queues, disconnects, and server lag. However, save for a few minor hiccups here and there, things went off without a hitch.

Eurogamer can report first-hand that for European players who stayed up from, let's say 11pm - 3:50am last night, the login queues were short and constantly moving. Those who were very keen to get in the moment servers went live ran into unclickable server selection boxes, but backing out and re-joining the short queue fixed this problem swiftly.

Once you got in, there was very little server lag save for a lost spell cast or two, nor were constant random disconnects that would boot you out into the cold (I didn't get disconnected once - a record). As far as WoW launches go, an incredibly smooth first day.

This was acknowledged by World of Warcraft developers, such as executive producer Holly Longdale who wrote on X: "At the risk of jinxing things, so far so goodish which is crazy by itself. The team prepared a lot since the wildness of Beta. And this launch was crazier than the insanity we imagined but thankfully the team built plans and contingencies. They are incredible in my opinion.".

Josh "Aggrend" Greenfield, a senior game designer on World of Warcraft Forever, addressed some minor issues that did pop up. These include a zone population problem: in basic terms the megaservers split players into different shards, and some of these felt a bit empty of players. There was also a quirk with the various big boats and zeppelins dotted around the map, which were busted. Temporary portals were added to provide a workaround.

"Thanks for everyone making this a great, super smooth launch," Greenfield wrote. "I’m going to head home and 'go to sleep' now. Yep, sleeping. Totally not playing WoW Forever until 3am. Nope."

The reaction to this silky smooth launch has some players flabbergasted. "I can't believe how smooth this launch is" is the title of Reddit user Arizhela's post, currently topping the WoW Forever board. They continue: "I fully expected to not be able to play today, but I logged in with no queue and no lag."

Another post, created in the early hours of this morning, is dubbed: "Never take a day off for launch, they said" in which a WoW player regrets not booking some time off from work this week, expecting problems. "You've been finessed son," replied user SnooWalruses3948, while SirePuns shared in the shock: "The advice was sound, but this time around the developers hired a witch I tell you. The code must’ve been witchcraft, the hardware must’ve been blessed by a witch as well."

It is unclear just how well World of Warcraft: Forever's launch was, given the unsocialable and employment-averse release time in the dead of night for us Europeans, but it follows a record-breaking beta period in which many hopped back into the MMO. Impressions from this beta were largely positive, the magic of the old MMO seemingly recaptured.

We're heading toward Path of Exile 2 going 1.0, just two years after the action-RPG first launched in early access. Once this happens the game will be free-to-play, but given its success thus far, a senior developer at Baldur's Gate 3 company Larian Studios believes Grinding Gear Games is already well and truly in the green.

He mentions as much on Twitter, in discussions over how many players Path of Exile 2 will attract once there's no price to try it out. "Path of Exile 2 is so fucking genius because they're selling so many copies it won't even matter if nobody buys anything when it goes free," Michael Douse, director of publishing at Larian, writes.

Those are big words when it comes to expansive action RPGs, but given the playerbase, I suspect plenty would agree. Path of Exile 2's peak concurrent player count is 578,562, and that's when charging for the game in early access.

The sky seems like the limit once the full 1.0 release is here. That's a healthy community, and those are positive numbers when you're a team hoping to grow the game over a number of years before putting it out into the world.

#3882. Sony have cancelled Fairgame$, once again reminding us that chasing live service big bucks basically never works

You know, I'm sure that Sony had every intention of following through on their intention to release 10 live service games by 2026, as they mentioned way back in 2022. Well, as far as an intention that's designed to please shareholders can go, anyway. And now here we are, almost five years on from that comment that continues to haunt them with the news Fairgame$ has been cancelled.

This comes from a report from Bloomberg, who shared that, thankfully, there are no planned job cuts due to the game being cancelled. In a statement, Sony said that, "The studio will shift its focus to collaborating with other development teams across PlayStation Studios, while also exploring new creative opportunities, though didn't go into detail as to who those other teams are.

Bloomberg were also privy to a note shared with developers at Haven Studios from executives Sean Decker and John Doyle that follows a recent test of the game: "While the test demonstrated strong operational excellence, live ops readiness and community engagement, player feedback and retention results were mixed and fell short of the goals we had set. Combined with challenging market conditions in the PVP shooter genre, we have made the difficult decision to cease development on the game."

Sony have, notably, failed to capitalise on the live service trend; I'm sure I don't need to remind you about Concord. Hell, this isn't even taking the end of Destiny 2 into consideration, once a driving force of live service games, or how Marathon has struggled to pick up an audience in the way that Sony may want it to. You just can't force a game to be popular, especially in a genre like shooters.

For those that either missed or forgot about Fairgame$, it was announced back in 2023 and was supposed to be a "competitive modern heist game where you team up to break into exotic locations and steal the cargo," all while taking on security and other, real people. Gameplay was never formally revealed, only a CGI trailer, and was set to come to PC as well as PlayStation. Bloomberg also noted that the game had been reworked multiple times since the announcement and was set to be re-revealed with a new name. Ultimately, it looks like Katharine was a little generous with her timeline of six months.

#3881. PlayStation sees record high player numbers and increased revenue for Q2 2026, and a lot of that success is down to Marvel's Wolverine

As part of today's (Thursday 5th November, 2026) financial results, Sony has confirmed that monthly active users, referred to as MAU, across both PlayStation 4 and 5, reached 127 million in September. This represents a seven percent growth year-on-year for the company, and sets a new record high.

In Layman's terms, this simply means that more people are engaged with the PlayStation ecosystem now than ever before. And it's not just that there are more people using machines and occasionally booting up their consoles; active play time also increased over the past quarter, too, with total logged play time increasing by four percent, year-on-year. As a result, Sony and PlayStation noted that its Game & Network Services division saw revenue grow by nine percent year-on-year, resulting in operating profit rising by 83 percent year-on-year.

Notably, despite its mixed reception, Marvel's Wolverine was name-checked as a driving force for the decent performance over the past quarter - but that shouldn't be a surprise for anyone that's actually been paying attention to how the game performed. The game sold through 2.4 million copies as of 4th November (so, in roughly 50 days). Ghost of Yotei, meanwhile, has sold through 3.3 million since its launch in October 2025.

More people playing consoles, and for longer - it must all be good news for Sony right? Well, not all the graphs are showing growth. PS5 hardware sales continue to gradually decline: in the reporting period, Sony sold 2.6 million PS5 consoles, down from 4 million in the same quarter in 2025. But, with 100 million PS5 units out in the wild, and 127 million PlayStation accounts across the whole ecosystem, Sony doesn't seem that worried: instead, the company is now focusing on converting those with active accounts into more viable customers.

Elsewhere in the results, we heard from Sony CFO Lin Tao that the PlayStation 6 is on track and "progressing as scheduled", with "solid progress" expected on the machine in 2027. Regarding those falling PS5 sales, Tao also referenced that, and says it's all part of the natural cycle of console launches and iteration. "Although new PS5 unit sales are gradually declining as expected at this stage of the console life cycle, the PlayStation platform continues to expand and grow in a stable manner," Tao explained. "[Next year,] we intend to make solid progress in preparing for the next-generation platform."

It must be encouraging for Sony to see this growth in this quarter, especially after all the bad press and furore around the company's decision to end the manufacturing of PlayStation discs by January 2028. It seems to be a core part of the gaming audience's understanding of game ownership, the decision has been widely contested as anti-consumer. It's caused a lot of bad blood with PlayStation players over the past six months, but - seemingly, given these results - that has translated to very little material impact on Sony's bottom line.

Despite its mixed reception, Marvel's Wolverine was September's top-selling new game in the US, making Sony launch revenues it hasn't seen since Helldivers 2

Deputy CEO Mattias Lilja is taking the reins in January.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Paradox Interactive is getting a new boss: Deputy CEO Mattias Lilja will take over from current CEO Fredrik Wester in January 2027, a move Paradox said "is a natural evolution of how the company is already led."

"My plan was never to be CEO for life. The goal was to build the foundation before passing the baton on for the next chapter in the company’s journey," Wester said in today's announcement.

"Since I returned as CEO, we’ve streamlined our strategy, rebuilt our pipeline and developed our commercial offering. Mattias has had a central role in laying this foundation, and now is the right time to hand over. Given his experience and vision, he is exceptionally well positioned to take the company to its next level."

As his statement implies, this is his second tenure as Paradox CEO: He held the position from 2009 to 2018, when he resigned and was replaced by Ebba Ljungerud. But Ljungerud's tenure was rocky, and she resigned in 2021 over "differing views on the company's strategy going forward," at which point Wester returned to the role.

In many ways, Lilja has been calling the CEO shots for a few years now anyway, while Wester's focus has increasingly been on Paradox's "long-term development and goals." And he, like Wester, is also a returnee: He left the company in 2020 after five years in various executive roles, but returned in 2021 along with Wester as "chief of staff." Lilja's LinkedIn profile says his primary duty was to "support the Paradox CEO in leading the executive team, aligning the strategic plan with the day to day operations," and that he would "act as the stand-in for the CEO when needed."

"I approach this role with great humility," Lilja said. "Paradox has a unique DNA that has made us one of the greats in deep and engaging strategy and management games. Now we’re stepping up the pace: we will make further investments in our core business, push the boundaries of our game design, work even more closely with our loyal players, develop more and better tools and services that benefit both modders and players, and continue to sharpen our ways of working and our organisation, with player value in focus."

Reaction among the Paradox community on Reddit seems guarded at this point, which is perhaps understandable given how it went the time the company got a new CEO. PC Gamer's Fraser Brown took a deep dive into that in his 2024 report on "the Dark Age of Paradox Interactive," which includes thoughts from Lilja on the "challenges" of success and what he saw as the future of Paradox.

From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews

Even back then, Lilja was clearly helping chart the company's course, and there's also some optimism among Paradox follower in the fact that he seems likely to carry on in Wester's footsteps—and an apparent understanding that Wester has been eyeing the door for a while now anyway.

Lilja will take over as Paradox CEO on January 4, 2027.

#3879. Sick BMX flips, colourful characters, a whole lot of mail and a charming raccoon dog await you in Tanuki: Pon's Summer, which you can pick up now

Right, today's been miserable thanks to the now hourly discourse we have to all take part in lest we be seen as approving of the current bad thing, how about something that looks simply pleasant? Today's the launch day for Tanuki: Pon's Summer, a delightfully vibrant mail delivery sim/Tony Hawk's Pro Skater but for bikes about restoring a shrine before the end of summer.

I've been enamoured by the vibe of Tanuki: Pon's Summer since it was announced in no small part because of how in some small ways it reminds me of Boku No Natsuyasumi, a cult-classic, Japan-only game series that's mostly just about hanging out in the Japanese countryside. This one isn't so lackadaisical, as you do have a job to do in delivering mail, but I think a similar spirit is there.

When it comes to delivering mail, there is a Death Strandingian element to it in your need to place your boxes on your BMX (which you can do sick tricks and flips on, of course) to maximise how much you can deliver. A bit less stressful than Kojima's joint, obviously, though elements are still there. Any money you earn from this gig can then be spent on restoring the shrine that you oh so love, which falls onto the sim side of things with the ability to fully customise how the shrine looks.

There are also a whole heap of minigames to perform that helps you get to know the locals. I'm talking baseball, sumo wrestling, working in a sushi restaurant and, of course, fishing. You can see bits of that in the launch trailer above, which comes with as 2010s an anime opening song you could wish for with some animation so good it makes me want an adaptation of the game. In time, perhaps! You can pick it up on Steam right here.

While Cyberpunk 2077 protagonist V is yours to shape, CD Projekt Red intentionally takes the wheel for narrative effect and to undermine your choices. If that feels uncomfortable, that's because it's supposed to.

Over on the ol' global town square, one fan points out that V states their preference not to smoke fairly in the game. Later on, as V's consciousness begins to merge with rocker-boy Johnny Silverhand, V smokes. It's not because they've got into the habit, but because Silverhand has done so for ages and your mind isn't entirely your own anymore.

The observation caught the attention of a very impressed quest lead, Pawel Sasko.

"Great eye my choom, that was exactly the intent — to show how slowly Johnny’s personality blends with V, through small subtle actions, and from the first confrontation when he tried to kill V transform this relationship into deep and meaningful bond, braided empathy and regret," he says.

Not everyone is on board, though. Some have replied to Sasko to say an RPG is, well, an RPG – that should mean your V is yours to shape entirely. For Sasko, though, that's even more reason to take away the sort of control you'd expect from the genre.

"But that was the point, it was meant to feel a little uncomfortable, what is happening to you," he says. "The game deals with terminal illness, it's not a voluntary state, we are using RPG game mechanics to illustrate it."

Feelings aside, it's cool that Cyberpunk 2077's small flourishes are still being uncovered and picked apart many years after launch. We've had expansions, Edgerunners-themed updates, and plenty of patches in between, but Cyberpunk 2077 has remained fairly complete narratively for a while, and as we head towards Cyberpunk 2, what better to mull over than narrative beats? I'm sure CDPR would rather people talk about that over how the game launched; that's for sure.

#3877. Nintendo game sales surge thanks to Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream, but Switch 2 hardware suffers big decline

Nintendo's latest financial earnings report is here, revealing healthy software sales thanks to the enormously popular Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream. Sales of Switch 2 hardware, however, are down.

As per Nintendo's 2nd Quarter fiscal earnings report, focusing on the three-month period ending 30th September 2026, Switch 2 hardware registered a big drop in sales during the first half of the current financial year (FY27).

Over that period, Nintendo sold 6.49m Switch 2 units and 1.27m units of the original Switch - equating to a 37.4 percent decline for Switch 2 and 32.7 percent decline for Switch 1 compared to the same period last year. Nintendo had previously forecast a decline in hardware sales, and the company still expects to sell 16.50m Switch 2 units by the end of the current fiscal year.

Nintendo software sales, on the other hand, saw a big year-on-year boost of 18.8 percent on Switch 2 (to 24.49m units) and a smaller increase of 6.8 percent on Switch 1. That's all thanks to the release of several popular first- and third-party titles over the first half of FY27. Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream was by far the most successful game with 8.81m units sold, followed by Rhythm Heaven Groove at 2.89m. Splatoon Raiders (the only Switch 2 exclusive of the three) sold 2.42m. Nintendo also highlighted a 60.5 percent year-on-year increase in digital game sales.

The increase in software unit sales and the "continued weakness of the Yen" couldn't prevent the overall business from declining by 15.3 percent year-on-year, however.

Other remaining releases in Nintendo' s current fiscal year include The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake (which launches today and was awarded five stars in Eurogamer's review), Switch 2 re-releases of Pikmin 2 and Xenoblade Chronicles 3, as well as Metroid Ravenous, which arrives early in 2027.

#3876. Keeping hold of Company of Heroes was essential for Relic to leave Sega, Relic CEO says – "Without it we would have been a dead studio"

In the nearly 30 years since they opened their doors, Relic have been an enormously influential studio. Responsible for lauded RTS series Homeworld, Dawn of War, and Company of Heroes, they also dabbled in other genres with third-person shooter The Outfit and the original Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine. Yet, despite this history, in 2024, when Relic were negotiating their sale from Sega to UK investment firm Emona Capita, CEO Justin Dowdeswell knew the rights to Company of Heroes had to be part of the deal. "Without it we would have been a dead studio," he tells me.

Without naming names Dowdeswell points out that there are "numerous examples" of studios that weren't able to survive on their name alone. Not only did Relic need the ability to make more games in the series that they were known for, but they also needed the income from back catalogue sales a series like Company of Heroes provides.

Dowdeswell joined Relic shortly after Sega acquired the studio in 2013. This was in the immediate aftermath of publisher THQ's bankruptcy auction, where studios and franchises were sold off to the highest bidder. While Sega bought the studio, they didn't buy the licenses to everything Relic had created. "The other games that Relic made – Homeworld, Impossible Creatures, The Outfit... formative games in many people's memory – they were all split up, scattered," Dowdeswell says. "I think that was... I won't say a tragedy, but it's unfortunate because Relic is the home of those games. It would have been great for them to stay with the studio."

Just as a hint of the messy history of acquisitions and auctions: this year we see Dawn of War 4 coming from studio King Art Games and published by Deep Silver. Deep Silver are a subdivision of Plaion, formerly called Koch Media, which was acquired by Embracer Group back when they were called THQ Nordic. Not that they were actually the THQ that originally published Relic's Dawn of War, Nordic Games renamed themselves THQ Nordic after they bought the THQ trademark at auction.

As for Homeworld, Borderlands developer Gearbox picked up the license to the sci-fi RTS in the bankruptcy auction, then contracted Blackbird Interactive's support on the remasters, before handing the latter lead development on Homeworld 3. That chain of events does have a more clear throughline to Relic's past however, as Blackbird was created by two of Relic's co-founders Rob Cunningham and Jon Aaron Kambeitz. (Speaking of studios struggling without the series they made their name with, Blackbird was on the verge of bankruptcy before Gearbox got in touch with the Homeworld work. So we very nearly existed in a world where they never got to make the brilliant Homeworld: Deserts of Kharak and Hardspace Shipbreaker.)

None of this is intended to be a knock on Dawn of War 4. From what I've played it's a very good Warhammer 40K RTS, if it perhaps sticks a little closely to the model laid down by Relic's original. What do I know, though, talking about their own games, Dowdeswell tells me that while "one of the messages to the studio is we can't just make [the same] things that we made 20 years ago and hope it goes well", re-releasing the 20-year-old Dawn of War sold very well for Relic and netted the team some very positive reviews on Steam. "There's a bit of a paradox there," he adds"

Anyway, this is all getting side-tracked. Back to holding onto Company of Heroes when separating from Sega. "Fighting for Company of Heroes when leaving Sega was crucial because I already lamented the fact that the other games didn't come with Relic," Dowdeswell says. "I couldn't really imagine a Relic where none of the games that the studio has made and was known for were any longer part of it."

Relic and new owner UK investment firm Emona Capital LLP were able to negotiate Company of Heroes as part of the sale from Sega and since then the studio has spent the past two years focusing largely on supporting the WW2 RTS and restoring their back catalogue. The most recent update is the massive 3.0 patch to mark the series' 20th anniversary. Which, among many changes, overhauls the Mediterranean-set RTS game's special effects, audio systems, NPC AI, and makes significant changes to the singleplayer grand strategy-inspired Italy campaign, as well as adding a whole set of autumn and winter-themed assets for community map makers. They've also released a series of DLCs adding new factions to Company of Heroes 3's skirmishes and multiplayer, re-released Dawn of War with a definitive edition and announced they're doing the same for the original Company of Heroes, along with Blackbird Interactive's help. Dowdeswell says foundation building masks a lot of the work going on behind the scenes: "We now self-publish all of this," he explains. "There were a number of things that we had to learn, skills we had to develop, capacity and capability that we had to build at the studio very, very quickly."

I ask if it was always the plan to focus on their back catalogue, or if they had plans to release new games. Dowdeswell says spending four years quietly working on a new game wasn't an option: "It's almost impossible to do it that way because of the current climate in the industry. We don't have a financial safety net." Though, the team do have larger ambitions. "We want to make new games, we want to provide a modern Relic game," Dowdeswell says. "That ambition to re-establish Relic as an innovator in this strategy space is a big part of what drives our creative direction on new games." Focusing on updating Company of Heroes 3, releasing DLC for the game, and making definitive editions of Dawn of War and the original Company of Heroes is what gets the studio to the place it can make a new game.

However, Dowdeswell resists any framing of Relic's work on Company of Heroes 3 as spinning their wheels or resting on their laurels while working toward a new game. He argues the game "sits in between" Relic's past and its future: "It's an established game that came out three years ago, but it's also a way for us to take some chances, experiment a little bit, and while doing that staying really closely connected to the players, That's what the idea was behind the updates because it was a way to have very quick iterations and touch points with players and provide, honestly, a way for us to fund everything in the future."

As to what Relic is making next, Dowdeswell wouldn't say. Though, he revealed trying genres besides real-time strategy was "almost a certainty", before adding "I don't think it's going to be a vast departure for where we are, so it will still be strategic gameplay. We're not going to go build a racer."

#3874. Mass Effect petition has enough signatures for the Canadian Government to potentially save BioWare

Following news of EA's decision to shut down iconic RPG studio BioWare, Canadian fans of the studio have escalated their grievances to the governmental level, calling on the Canadian Government to step in and save the Canadian studio from closure, seemingly after Canada's New Democratic Party leader Avi Lewis called on the government to do so.

Fans have submitted a petition to the Canadian House of Commons arguing for the government to find a way for BioWare to continue, such as through funding that allows the studio to buy the Mass Effect and other IPs and go independent.

The petition, number e-7898, argues that "BioWare is one of Canada's most important cultural exports" and that the studio's closure by its American parent company "represents an immense loss to and possibly a targeted attack on Canada's cultural legacy."

"BioWare's productions champion the values of inclusivity, tolerance, democracy, justice, and civil rights that are at the centre of Canada's national identity," it continued.

The petition opened for signatures on 4th of November, and has already amassed 1,700 signatures. By law, petitions that surpass 500 valid signatures from Canadian citizens or residents are entered into the House of Commons' agenda, meaning they will be presented in front of the parliament.

As encouraging as that may be, it's worth keeping in mind that it may not result in meaningful change. Even if the Canadian Government agrees with the petition's goals, it cannot force EA to sell BioWare or its various IPs.

EA notably didn't shop the studio around before closing it down, and the publisher has a history of closing down owned studios rather than selling them off. EA has also kept the IPs of its various shuttered studios.

The community's reaction to BioWare's closure has taken different forms. Hundreds of thousands signed a different petition to save Mass Effect. The people behind the movement have purchased billboards in Times Square in New York City to advertise it, with plans for more outside The Game Awards ceremony in December.

Meanwhile, former BioWare developers have spoken about the last days of BioWare, and the work they've poured into Mass Effect Universe, the studio's final project before it was shuttered.
